Deathknell Triggers: Both units have Deathknell abilities. These triggers are added to the chain as pending items before the units are moved to the trash.

Chain Resolution: You are the controller of these triggers. You choose the order in which to add them to the chain.

Resolving Glasc Mixologist: When you resolve the Deathknell trigger from Glasc Mixologist, you are instructed to play a unit from your trash with an energy cost of 3 or less.

Playing the Unit: Because the unit that died simultaneously is now in your trash, it is a legal target for the Deathknell effect of Glasc Mixologist. You may play it from your trash to the battlefield, ignoring its energy cost.

Important Nuance: Attacker vs. Defender
Whether you can successfully play the unit to a specific battlefield depends on your status at that location:

If you are the Defender: You already control the battlefield, so you can play the unit there to maintain your control (FAQ #9149).

If you are the Attacker: You do not control the battlefield until the showdown is resolved and you have successfully conquered it. Therefore, you cannot play a unit to that battlefield during the combat cleanup phase (FAQ #9479).

question: Does After Showdown heal all units everywhere?
answer:
Yes, at the end of a combat showdown, all units everywhere in play heal all damage marked on them simultaneously.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #6111 and CR 463.1.a.1, this healing occurs during the Resolution Step of a combat as part of the Combat Special Cleanup. It applies to all units on the board, regardless of their location (at the battlefield, in base, or elsewhere) and regardless of whether they participated in the combat.

Important distinctions:

Combat vs. Non-Combat: This healing only triggers after combat showdowns (contested battlefields where units from both players are present). Units do not heal after a non-combat showdown (e.g., when a battlefield is contested, but only one player has units there).

Healing at End of Turn: Additionally, all units heal all damage at the end of the turn during the Ending Phase (Rule 317.2.b).

Damage is separate from Might: Note that damage marked on a unit does not reduce its Might value; it is tracked separately, and units are only destroyed when marked damage equals or exceeds their Might.

question: If I use sacrifice on a might unit and then save it using Tactical Retreat do I draw 2?
answer:
Yes, you do draw 2 cards.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9425, when you play Sacrifice and use Tactical Retreat to save the unit intended as the sacrifice cost, the following occurs:

Playing the Spell: You announce Sacrifice and choose your Mighty unit as the target for the "kill" cost.

Paying Costs: You attempt to pay the cost by killing the unit.

Replacement: Tactical Retreat's replacement effect intercedes. Instead of the unit going to the trash, it is healed, exhausted, and recalled to your base.

Cost Completion: Per Rule 357.2.a, costs that are replaced by replacement effects are still considered paid. Therefore, the cost for Sacrifice is successfully paid.

Resolution: Sacrifice resolves, and you draw 2 cards and channel 1 rune.

Your unit survives because the replacement effect of Tactical Retreat changed the outcome of the "kill" instruction (the cost) without preventing the spell from successfully completing its cost payment and resolving its effect.

question: Does Deathknell happen after unit heal from Showdown?
answer:
To clarify the interaction between Deathknell abilities and healing after a combat showdown, the healing occurs before Deathknell abilities resolve.

According to the official sequence defined in CR 463 and clarified in RiftJudge FAQ #9514 and FAQ #9677, the process is as follows:

The Correct Sequence (Combat Cleanup)

Combat Damage Step: Combat damage is dealt to units (CR 462.2.d).

Triggering Deathknell: As part of the Combat Special Cleanup, units with lethal damage trigger their Deathknell abilities immediately before they are killed. These are added to the chain as Pending Items (Rule 808.1.d.2, Rule 383.2.c.3).

Killing Units: Units with lethal damage are moved to the trash (CR 323.4).

Healing: Surviving units are healed (CR 463.1.a.1).

Resolution: The game returns to the FEPR (Finalize, Execute, Pass, Resolve) process. The pending Deathknell triggers that were added to the chain are now finalized and resolved (Rule 808.1.d.3, FAQ #9514).

Key Takeaways

Healing First: Units survive the Combat Damage Step are healed before any Deathknell abilities resolve.

No "Saving" Units: Because units are killed for having lethal damage during the cleanup phase (Step 3 above), a Deathknell effect cannot be used to "save" a unit that already took lethal combat damage.

No "Finishing Off": Because healing occurs (Step 4) before the Deathknell triggers resolve (Step 5), a Deathknell ability cannot be used to finish off an enemy unit that survived the combat damage, as that damage will be cleared by the healing step before the Deathknell effect can be executed.

In summary, while the Deathknell trigger is placed on the chain during the cleanup, the resolution of the effect—where the card text actually executes—happens only after the healing step is completed.

question: Can I use a Hidden Wages of Pain on an enemy at a different battlefield?
answer:
No, you cannot.

According to CR 811.1.d.2, if a spell played from Hidden chooses any targets, those targets must be chosen from among options at the same battlefield where that card was hidden.

Because Wages of Pain requires you to choose a target ("Deal 3 to a unit at a battlefield"), you are strictly limited to targeting units located at the specific battlefield where you hid the card. You cannot use it to target a unit at a different battlefield.

question: Does Imperial Decree trigger the moment something takes damage?
answer:
Yes, Imperial Decree triggers the moment a unit takes damage.

According to the RiftJudge FAQs (#1917, #5341, #8633), Imperial Decree creates a lasting effect for the turn that functions as a triggered ability. When any unit takes damage while this effect is active, the trigger fires immediately.

Here is how the interaction works:

The Trigger Event: When a unit takes damage, the event of "taking damage" acts as the trigger condition.

The Chain: The trigger is placed on the chain. Because it is a triggered ability that uses the chain, it provides a window for players to play [REACTION] cards (such as flipping a hidden Zhonya's Hourglass) before the ability resolves.

Resolution: Once the chain resolves (or if no reactions are played), the effect executes, and the damaged unit is killed.

Important Nuances:

Not Retroactive: As clarified in RiftJudge FAQ #2873 and #8633, Imperial Decree only triggers for damage taken after it has resolved. It does not look back to kill units that were already damaged before the spell was cast.

Damage Event vs. State: It triggers on the event of receiving damage, not simply because a unit is currently in a damaged state.

Combat Assignment: Imperial Decree does not change standard combat damage assignment rules (you must still assign full might to a unit before moving to the next). However, because it kills units upon taking any amount of damage, it is effectively used to clear enemy boards by sending units into combat sequentially.

question: Can you attach multiple Gear to the same unit?
answer:
Yes, you can attach multiple pieces of gear to the same unit.

According to RiftJudge FAQ 9165, there is no limit to the number of equipment cards that can be attached to a single unit at the same time. As long as you have the resources to pay the costs and the equipment is not already attached (because you cannot activate the Equip ability of a piece of gear that is already attached, per Rule 730), you may continue to attach additional gear to that unit.

question: If I control a Battlefield and have Glass Mixologist and Xin Zhao at the same Battlefield die by combat, can I revive that same Xin Zhao to that same Battlefield?
answer:
Yes, you can revive that same Xin Zhao to that same battlefield.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9620 and FAQ #8739, when your Glasc Mixologist dies during combat, its Deathknell ability triggers and is placed on the chain as a pending item during the cleanup process. Because the game pauses to resolve this chain before finalizing the combat result and control checks, you are permitted to play a unit from your trash to that battlefield.

Sequence of Events

Combat Damage Step: Both Glasc Mixologist and Xin Zhao take lethal damage and die.

Deathknell Trigger: Glasc Mixologist's Deathknell triggers and is placed on the chain.

Resolution: The chain resolves. You resolve the Deathknell effect, which allows you to play a unit with cost no more than [3] and no more than [A] from your trash.

Unit Entry: You choose Xin Zhao (Energy cost 3) from your trash and play it to the battlefield where it just died.

Combat Cleanup: The game proceeds to finish the combat cleanup. Because you now have a unit present at the battlefield, the battlefield will not become uncontrolled, and the "no result" or control determination will factor in your newly revived Xin Zhao.

Note: This is based on the mechanics of Deathknell and battlefield control as established in the provided RiftJudge FAQs (specifically #9620 and #8739).

question: Can the Fiora legend buff a unit if it's already a 5 might card?
answer:
No, Fiora (Grand Duelist) cannot trigger her ability when a unit that is already at 5 or more Might (already Mighty) receives a buff.

According to Rule 709: "A Unit 'becomes Mighty' at the moment its Might changes from being less than 5 to being 5 or greater."

As clarified in RiftJudge FAQ #9584, if a unit is already at 5 or greater Might, it is already considered "Mighty" (Rule 708). Increasing its Might further does not change its status from "not Mighty" to "Mighty," so it does not trigger Fiora's Legend ability.

question: If my Ferrous Forerunner dies in combat with Rek'Sai on base, do I have to pay for Mechs to be accelerated?
answer:
Yes, you must pay the Accelerate cost if you want the Mech tokens to enter the battlefield ready.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ (#8671, #9360), here is how this interaction works:

Triggering: When Ferrous Forerunner dies, its [Deathknell] ability triggers and is placed on the chain.

Playing the Tokens: When the Deathknell ability resolves, it instructs you to "play" two Mech unit tokens.

Granting Accelerate: Because these tokens are being played from an ability (not from your hand), Rek'Sai, Breacher's ability grants them [Accelerate].

Optional Cost: Accelerate is an optional additional cost (Rule 805.2). To have a unit enter the battlefield ready, you must pay the Accelerate cost—which is 1 Energy and 1 Power—as part of the process of playing the token.

Result:

If you pay the cost for a token, it enters the board ready.

If you do not pay the cost for a token, it enters the board exhausted (the default state for units entering play).

You pay this cost separately for each token, meaning you can choose to pay for both, one, or neither.

question: In the beginning of the game, after you roll to see who goes first, are the battlefields revealed and then the winning player picks who goes first? Or what is the order of beginning a game?
answer:
According to the official rules, battlefields are revealed before determining turn order. The winning player of the "roll to go first" (or any other fair random method) then chooses whether they wish to play first or last.

Based on the Core Rules and official FAQs, here is the official Start of Game sequence:

Legend selection

Champion selection

Battlefield selection and placement: Battlefields are chosen and placed face-up in the Battlefield Zone simultaneously. They are public information once placed.

Determine turn order: Players use a fair random method (such as a dice roll) to designate the first player.

Choose play order: The designated player chooses whether they wish to go first or last.

Draw cards (each player draws 4).

Mulligans (starting with the player going first).

Important Clarification:
As noted in the RiftJudge FAQs, it is a common error to hide battlefields until after determining turn order, but this is incorrect. Because battlefields are public information as soon as they are placed, they must be revealed before anyone makes the decision to play first or last. If you are playing a Best of 3 match, this procedure is repeated for every game, with the loser of the previous game being the one who makes the choice of play order (after battlefields are already revealed).

question: Can you sacrifice on Temporary Death?
answer:
Yes, you can.

When a unit with Temporary dies at the start of your Beginning Phase, it creates a chain, which allows you to play [Reaction] speed abilities and effects in response to that death trigger. If you control a card that requires a sacrifice as a cost to activate its ability or play it, you can use that unit as the sacrifice in response to the Temporary death trigger before the unit is removed from the board.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #6422, Temporary is a triggered ability that creates a chain, allowing players to respond with [Reaction] speed effects.

How it works:

Trigger: At the start of your Beginning Phase, the Temporary ability triggers and is placed on the chain.

Closed State: Because there is an item on the chain, the game enters a "Closed State."

Response: You can use your [Reaction] speed ability, paying the cost—which includes sacrificing the unit—to place your effect on top of the chain.

Resolution: Because the chain resolves in LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) order, your sacrifice ability resolves first. Your unit is sacrificed to pay the cost of your effect, and then the original Temporary trigger resolves. Since the unit is already gone (sacrificed), the "Kill" instruction of the Temporary ability will simply fail to find its target (it becomes an impossible instruction) and nothing further happens to that unit.

This is a common way to extract extra value from a unit that is about to die to its own Temporary effect.

question: So if my Yone took damage and is from a 5 to a 4, and I move it to an empty battlefield, after gaining a point for Conquer, do I also heal, and then use his ability? Or because there was no defender, there was no combat, does he stay at 4?
answer:
To address your question regarding Yone, damage, and combat:

1. Does Yone heal?

No, Yone does not heal.
As clarified in RiftJudge FAQ #9649, there is a critical distinction between a combat showdown and an open showdown:

Combat Showdown: Occurs when a unit moves to an opponent-controlled battlefield. This triggers combat, which includes a "Combat Cleanup" step where all units heal.

Open Showdown: Occurs when a unit moves to an empty (uncontrolled) battlefield. This is a showdown, but it is not combat. Because it is not combat, there is no combat cleanup, and therefore no healing occurs.

Moving to an empty battlefield allows you to conquer it and score, but it does not trigger the healing effects associated with the combat cleanup step.

2. How much damage does Yone's ability deal?

Yone deals damage equal to his full Might value, regardless of the damage marked on him.
As established in RiftJudge FAQ #6749, #5165, and #1193, damage marked on a unit does not reduce its Might. Might and damage are separate concepts:

A unit’s Might remains constant regardless of damage marked on it.

If your Yone has a base Might of 5, he remains a 5 Might unit even if he has damage marked on him.

When his ability resolves, he uses his current Might value to determine the damage dealt, not a reduced value.

Summary of the Sequence

Move Yone: You move Yone to an empty battlefield.

Conquer: You gain control of the battlefield and score a point.

Trigger Yone: Yone's ability triggers (as noted in FAQ #8405, he triggers at the end of a noncombat showdown in which he conquers).

Resolve Ability: Yone's ability goes on the chain. Upon resolution, it checks his current Might, which is not reduced by damage markers.

Status: Yone remains on the board with the damage markers still on him, as no combat cleanup occurred to heal him.

Note: I could not fully verify the specific mechanical claim that Yone's ability deals damage equal to his Might against the retrieved rules.

question: Does the damage on a unit from Challenge units fighting each other stick around?
answer:
Yes, the damage dealt by Challenge persists on the units involved until it is removed.

According to RiftJudge FAQ 7781, damage from Challenge remains on units until either combat occurs on any battlefield (which triggers a Combat Cleanup) or the turn ends.

Key points to remember:

Healing: Units do not heal immediately after using Challenge because Challenge is not considered combat (RiftJudge FAQ 7008).

Persistence: The damage persists on the units even if they do not participate in any subsequent combat during the turn.

Combat Cleanup: If combat happens on any battlefield, damage is removed from all units on the board during the resulting Combat Cleanup, regardless of whether those specific units were involved in the combat (RiftJudge FAQ 4225).

End of Turn: Any remaining damage on units is cleared at the end of the turn (Rule 143.3.b.1).

question: If you're not so fast an overzealous fan, does the fan still die from defending?
answer:
Yes, if you use Not So Fast to counter Overzealous Fan's triggered ability, the Overzealous Fan still dies.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #8702 (which reflects the current Unleashed rules update), the "kill me" instruction in Overzealous Fan's text is a cost within instructions that must be paid upfront to finalize the ability onto the chain.

Sequence of Events

Trigger Condition Met: Overzealous Fan gains the Defender designation and the ability triggers.

Payment and Finalization: To place the ability on the chain, its controller must pay the cost by killing the Overzealous Fan. The fan is now in the trash.

Ability Added to Chain: With the cost paid, the triggered ability is finalized and placed on the chain as a pending item.

Reaction Phase: The opponent (or the active player) may now play Not So Fast to target and counter that triggered ability.

Resolution: Not So Fast resolves, countering the Overzealous Fan's ability. The ability is cleared from the chain and its effect (moving an attacking unit) does not happen.

Key Clarification

Because the "kill me" requirement is a mandatory cost paid to put the ability onto the chain, the Overzealous Fan is already dead by the time your opponent has the opportunity to play Not So Fast. Countering the ability prevents the effect (moving the attacking unit) from occurring, but it does not "bring back" or save the Overzealous Fan that was already killed to pay the cost.

question: If I stun a unit to prevent damage once in a showdown, do we commence combat a second time without healing taking place in between calculating total might? Example: 5 might, counterstrike proc, into 8 might, I assume takes 5, and triggering a second round of damage calculation, 5 into 3?
answer:
No, a second round of combat does not occur.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #6276, if units from both players remain at the end of a showdown (such as when a unit is stunned and survives), another showdown does not start. Instead, the attackers are simply recalled back to their base.

Why this happens:

Combat is not iterative: Combat damage is dealt exactly once during the "Combat Damage Step" (CR 462.1). There is no mechanic that allows combat to "repeat" or "re-trigger" just because a unit was stunned or survived damage.

Stun mechanics: As specified in CR 424.1.b and 423.1.c, a stunned unit does not contribute its Might to damage in the combat damage step, but it still requires full lethal damage to be destroyed.

Outcome: Because the stunned unit does not contribute Might, it deals 0 damage to the opponent. However, if the opposing unit fails to deal damage equal to or greater than the stunned unit's full Might, the stunned unit survives. Once the damage is resolved and the units are still on the board, the combat concludes, and the attacker is recalled to base.

Your example scenario—where you stun a unit and expect a second, separate round of damage calculation—is not supported by the rules. The combat resolves in one single damage-dealing step, regardless of whether a unit is stunned.

question: If I own 0 battlefields and I'm 1 point from winning but I use Hostile Takeover on an enemy unit, do I score a hold point and win the game?
answer:
No, you do not win the game by scoring a "Hold" point. You would potentially win the game through a Conquer point, but not a Hold point.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9236, using Hostile Takeover to take control of an opponent's only unit at a battlefield does not count as "holding" that battlefield. Instead, it initiates a noncombat showdown, which results in you establishing control and performing a Conquer.

Here is the breakdown of why you cannot win via a "Hold" point in this scenario:

Hold vs. Conquer: "Hold" points are only awarded during your Beginning Phase (CR 466.2). Using a spell like Hostile Takeover during your Main Phase to seize a battlefield results in a "Conquer" (CR 466.1), not a "Hold."

Scoring the Win: While you would gain a point for the Conquer (if you haven't already scored that battlefield this turn), this does not satisfy the requirement for a "Hold" victory.

The Victory Condition: If this Conquer grants you the final point needed to reach the Victory Score, you will win the game. However, it is explicitly classified as a Conquer victory, not a Hold victory.

Summary of your sequence:

Hostile Takeover resolves: You take control of the unit.

Noncombat Showdown begins: You become the controller of the battlefield.

Conquer: Because you just gained control and haven't scored that battlefield yet this turn, you gain 1 point (CR 466.1).

Victory: If this point brings you to the required Victory Score, you win the game at that moment (CR 469).

You do not score a "Hold" point, as hold points are strictly awarded at the start of your turn for units already present there.

question: Does a countered card count for Legion or for Chemtech Cask?
answer:
To determine if a countered card counts for Legion or for the ability of Chemtech Cask, we must look at the specific requirements for each.

1. Does a countered card count for Legion?

Yes. According to RiftJudge FAQ #9461, #9463, and #9650, a card counts toward satisfying Legion requirements as soon as it is Finalized on the chain.

The Sequence: When you play a card, it is a "Pending Chain Item" until you choose targets and pay all costs. At that point, it becomes a "Finalized Chain Item."

Interaction: Legion checks if a card has been Finalized on the turn (Rule 812.1.c). Since countering occurs after the card has been finalized, the Legion condition is already satisfied for that turn, even if the card is subsequently countered and removed from the chain (CR 426.1.a).

2. Does a countered card count for Chemtech Cask?

No. Based on the text of Chemtech Cask, a countered card does not trigger its ability.

Card Text: "When you play a spell on an opponent's turn, you may exhaust me to play a Gold gear token exhausted."

The Ruling: While Legion relies on the "Finalized" state of a card, Chemtech Cask relies on the action of "playing" a spell. According to CR 426.1.b, "A card that is Countered is not considered to have been played."

Reasoning: Because a countered spell is not considered to have been played, the trigger condition for Chemtech Cask ("When you play a spell...") is never met. Therefore, the ability of Chemtech Cask cannot be activated if the spell it would have responded to is countered.

Summary

Legion: Satisfied by the act of finalizing a card on the chain, regardless of whether that card is later countered.

Chemtech Cask: Does not trigger, because a countered card is not considered to have been "played."

Note: I could not fully verify the ruling regarding Chemtech Cask against the retrieved rules.

question: If I trigger Overzealous Fan, can I still play an action?
answer:
Yes, you can still play an action after triggering Overzealous Fan's ability.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #8798 and FAQ #9694, a combat showdown does not end immediately when a unit is moved or removed from the battlefield (such as by Overzealous Fan). The showdown continues until both players pass consecutively with focus on an empty chain. Even if Overzealous Fan is killed, the showdown remains active, and you retain the opportunity to play other [ACTION] or [REACTION] cards provided you have the focus to do so.

Understanding the Timing (Unleashed Update)

The rules regarding the "kill me" cost for Overzealous Fan were updated in the Unleashed patch. Based on RiftJudge FAQ #8702 and FAQ #9611, the interaction functions as follows:

Trigger Condition Met: When Overzealous Fan gains the "Defender" designation during a combat showdown, its ability triggers.

Optional Choice: Because the ability text says "you may," the ability is optional (Rule 383.3.a).

Paying the Cost: If you choose to use the ability, you must kill Overzealous Fan upfront as a cost to place the ability on the chain (Rule 383.3.b.1).

Summary: Because the showdown persists after the Fan's ability triggers, resolves, or is countered, you are free to continue playing actions until the showdown officially concludes by both players passing priority on an empty chain.

Note: I could not fully verify the specific mechanical state definitions referenced in the draft against the retrieved rules.

question: For Relentless Pursuit does "when I conquer you may move me to base" effect remain for the rest of the turn?
answer:
Yes, the effect granted by Relentless Pursuit—"When I conquer, you may move me to my base"—remains active on that unit for the rest of the turn.

As specified on the card, the effect explicitly states: "This turn, that unit has 'When I conquer, you may move me to my base.'"

Because it is a continuous effect with a duration of "this turn," it will apply every time that unit successfully conquers a battlefield for the remainder of the turn (subject to the standard restriction that you can only score each battlefield once per turn, as per RiftJudge FAQ #7610 and RiftJudge FAQ #9258).

question: If I start combat and play Counter Strike, then it resolves. The chain is empty. Is it still my priority? Can I play first still, or is it impossible after I start combat and start a chain?
answer:
No, it is not your priority, and you cannot start another chain immediately.

According to Rule 340.2.a and RiftJudge FAQ #1968, during a showdown, once the chain resolves and the turn returns to an Open State, focus automatically passes to your opponent.

Here is the breakdown of your situation:

Opening the Showdown: You initiate combat. You gain the "Attacker" designation and gain Focus.

Starting a Chain: You play Counter Strike (or another action) to start a chain. Because you started the chain, it is now a Closed State.

Chain Resolves: The chain resolves, and Counter Strike creates its replacement effect.

Priority and Focus: Once the chain is empty and the state returns to Open, Focus automatically passes to the defender (your opponent).

Can you play again?
Yes, but you must wait. After your opponent gains Focus, they have the opportunity to either play an action (starting a new chain) or pass. If they pass, Focus returns to you, and you can then play another action if you wish. Both players must pass consecutively without starting a new chain for the showdown to proceed to the Combat Damage Step (as detailed in RiftJudge FAQ #3636 and FAQ #4166).

In short: You cannot act twice in a row. You must allow your opponent the opportunity to respond to the state of the board after your first chain resolves.

question: Does Sun Disk Legion tap after playing itself?
answer:
No, you cannot play Sun Disc as the first card of your turn and immediately exhaust it to activate its Legion ability.

Clarifying the Requirement

While some legacy FAQ content has caused confusion regarding whether a card counts itself toward its own Legion requirement, official rules clarify that it does not:

Rule 812.1.c states: "As long as a card different than the one with the Legion ability has been Finalized on the same turn then the Dependent Ability is Active."

Rule 812.1.b.1 clarifies that Legion is functionally shorthand for: "If you have played another card this turn..."

FAQ #8715 and FAQ #9616 confirm that Sun Disc does not count as "another card" for its own Legion requirement.

Therefore, you must play at least one other card during the turn before the Legion condition is satisfied and you can successfully exhaust Sun Disc to gain its benefit.

Correct Sequence for Sun Disc

To use Sun Disc successfully, follow this sequence during your Main Phase:

Play a different card: Play any other Main Deck card. This satisfies the Legion requirement for the remainder of the turn.

Play Sun Disc: If not already in play, you may play Sun Disc.

Exhaust Sun Disc: Because you have already finalized "another" card this turn, the Legion ability is active. Exhaust Sun Disc while the game state is "Open."

Play your unit: The next unit you play this turn will enter the battlefield ready.

Important Note: If you attempt to exhaust Sun Disc before playing another card, the Legion ability is inactive. According to the rules on dependent keywords, an inactive ability cannot be activated.

Note: I could not fully verify the interaction regarding payment of costs for inactive abilities against the retrieved rules.

question: Does Thundersong cancel out a Hourglass's hidden?
answer:
Yes, Brynhir Thundersong effectively prevents an opponent from playing a hidden card for the remainder of the turn once its ability resolves.

According to FAQ #5027: "The opponent cannot reveal hidden cards this turn after you play Brynhir Thundersong. Cards from hidden are also played, so Brynhir's effect prevents revealing them."

Timing and Interactions

Because playing a card from hidden uses the chain (Rule 811.1.c.3), you can still interact with Brynhir Thundersong when it is played:

Opponent plays Brynhir Thundersong: The unit enters play.

"When you play me" trigger: Brynhir’s ability is added to the chain.

Window for Response (The "Hidden" Window): Because the chain is open, you can play your hidden Zhonya's Hourglass in response to Brynhir's triggered ability.

Resolution: Once Brynhir’s triggered ability resolves, its effect ("opponents can't play cards this turn") takes hold. At that point, you are barred from playing further cards from hidden for the rest of the turn (FAQ #7748).

Summary: Brynhir Thundersong does not remove or destroy your hidden card; it simply restricts your ability to play it after her ability has resolved. You must respond to the trigger of Brynhir entering play if you wish to use your hidden card on that turn.

question: Does opponent plays Mirror Image, I bounce the chosen unit back to hand. Does Mirror Image still activate with copied unit?
answer:
When your opponent plays Mirror Image and you return the chosen unit to their hand, Mirror Image still resolves, but the resulting Reflection token will not successfully copy the unit.

1. Chain and Targeting

When your opponent plays Mirror Image, it is placed on the chain, and they must choose a target unit. If you respond by playing a spell or ability to bounce that unit to their hand before Mirror Image resolves, the target is removed from the board.

2. Resolution Sequence

According to Rule 359.3.e.6 and Rule 359.3.e.7, instructions that cannot be followed due to missing targets are ignored.

Mirror Image resolves.

The instruction "Play a ready Reflection unit token to your base" is executed. A 0 Might Reflection token enters play at your opponent's base.

The instruction "It becomes a copy of that unit" attempts to execute. Because the original unit is no longer on the board, the instruction fails to find a valid target and is ignored.

The final instruction "Give it [Temporary]" is executed.

3. Resulting Token

The Reflection token remains on the board as a 0 Might unit with the [Temporary] keyword. Because the copy effect failed, it does not inherit any other traits, stats, or rules text from the original unit. Because it was given [Temporary], it will still be killed at the start of your opponent's next Beginning Phase (as per Rule 816.1.b).

Note: I could not fully verify the specific text of the Mirror Image card or the resulting token's keywords against the retrieved rules.

question: Does Deflect work with Forbidding Waste Battlefield?
answer:
No, Deflect does not interact with the ability of the Forbidding Waste battlefield.

Why Deflect does not apply:

Deflect's Targeting Requirement: According to Rule 809.1.c, the Deflect keyword specifically applies to spells and abilities an opponent controls that "choose" the unit with Deflect.

Forbidding Waste's Ability: The ability of Forbidding Waste imposes a -2 Might penalty on a unit that is defending alone.

Nature of the Ability: This is a continuous static effect generated by the battlefield. It does not "choose" or "target" the units affected by it; it simply imposes a penalty on any unit that meets the condition of defending alone.

Summary

Because the Forbidding Waste ability does not select or choose a target—functioning instead as a global condition that applies automatically to any unit in that state—it does not satisfy the requirements to trigger the Deflect keyword.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: In a 2v2 if an opponent controls a battlefield with a Jayce and I charm their teammate's Akshan into the base that the Jayce controls, do they fight each other and both die?
answer:
No, this play is illegal.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #1089 and RiftJudge FAQ #260, it is illegal to move a unit to a battlefield occupied by a teammate. Teammates can never have units at the same battlefield. Therefore, you cannot play Charm to move an opponent's Akshan into a battlefield controlled by their teammate who controls Jayce.

Because the move is illegal, the Akshan will not move, no showdown will occur, and neither unit will die.

question: Does Janna's "move an enemy unit" when played mean choose, aka pay deflect cost?
answer:
Yes, moving an enemy unit with Janna, Savior's ability triggers Deflect because it requires you to "choose" a specific enemy unit.

Why it triggers Deflect

According to Rule 355.7 and Rule 809.1.d, Deflect is a mandatory additional cost imposed on any spell or ability that chooses or targets a permanent with Deflect.

Targeting vs. Affecting: While Janna's ability does not explicitly use the word "target," it instructs you to "move up to one enemy unit." Because you must select a specific enemy unit on the board to move, you are choosing that unit.

Mandatory Cost: If you select an enemy unit that has Deflect, you must pay the Deflect cost as an additional cost to place that ability on the chain.

Sequence and Interaction

Playing Janna: When you play Janna, Savior, she enters the board, and her "When you play me" ability is placed on the chain.

Making Choices: You decide whether to use the ability to move a unit. If you choose to move a unit, you must select which enemy unit to move at this time.

Deflect Payment: If the unit you chose has Deflect, you must pay the Deflect cost (in addition to any other costs for the ability) to finalize the ability on the chain.

Inability to Pay: If you cannot afford the Deflect cost, you cannot choose that unit as a target (FAQ #8660).

Summary: Because the ability requires you to select a specific unit to move, it acts as a targeted ability for the purposes of the Deflect keyword.

This is my interpretation based on the mechanics of targeting and mandatory additional costs defined in Rule 355.7 and Rule 809.1. No official FAQ exists for this specific interaction with Janna, but it follows the established rulings for other cards with similar "move an enemy unit" effects (see RiftJudge FAQ #8505).

question: If I have 2 Guardian Angels equipped to 1 unit and it dies, do both Guardian Angels get burned to recall my unit?
answer:
No, both Guardian Angel gears are not destroyed. Only one Guardian Angel will be destroyed when the unit would die.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ #1622 and FAQ #9026:

Replacement Effect: Guardian Angel functions as a replacement effect. When the unit would die, the effect replaces that "death" event with "kill this Guardian Angel instead."

Single Application: When the unit would die, you choose one of the Guardian Angel gears to apply its replacement effect. Once that effect resolves, the unit is healed, exhausted, and recalled to your base.

Death Prevented: Because the unit is recalled to the base, it never actually "dies." Since the death event has been prevented, the second Guardian Angel's trigger condition is no longer met, and it remains attached to the unit in your base.

This interaction is consistent with the rule that you can only replace the same death event once.

question: Can you target gear on Ruin Runner? Or is it protected by the card?
answer:
Yes, you can target gear attached to Ruin Runner.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9699:

Q: Can you target equipment attached to Ruin Runner with Salvage?
A: Ruling: Yes. When you play Salvage, you are choosing a gear as the target, not the unit it is attached to. Ruin Runner's protection ability ("I can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities") only prevents the unit itself from being chosen, not the equipment attached to it.

Nuances:

Targeting gear attached to a unit does not count as targeting the unit itself.

If a spell or ability specifically requires you to choose a unit (like Angled Shot), it would still be prevented by Ruin Runner's protection ability.

question: Hey, I have a question. I'm defending a camp with a traveling merchant, enemy player attacks that camp with an overzealous fan. In his priority attacking player plays a spinning axe. Is it possible for defending player to answer to that spinning axe with a gust?
answer:
Yes, you can respond to the Spinning Axe with Gust.

According to the Showdown Timing Flowchart, once a Showdown has begun, the state is generally "Closed" when items are on the chain. During this time, players can alternate playing [Reaction] cards.

Here is the sequence of events based on your situation:

Initial Chain: The Overzealous Fan moves into the battlefield. Its "When I defend" trigger (if you were the one defending with it) or "When I attack" trigger (if it is the attacker) goes on the chain. (Note: Per your description, the Overzealous Fan is the attacker).

Attacker's Action: Once the initial chain resolves and the state becomes Open, the Attacker (with Focus) plays Spinning Axe. The state becomes "Closed."

Your Response: As the Defender, you have the opportunity to add a [Reaction] to the chain. Gust is a [Reaction] spell. You play Gust targeting the Overzealous Fan.

Why this works:

Reaction Timing: [Reaction] spells can be played whenever a chain is "Closed" (meaning an item is already on the chain waiting to resolve) or when it is "Open."

LIFO Resolution: Per Riftbound rules, the chain resolves Last-In, First-Out (LIFO). Because Gust was the last item added to the chain, it will resolve first, returning the Overzealous Fan to the hand before the Spinning Axe has a chance to attach to it (or resolve).

This interaction is consistent with the established timing rules for Riftbound, as seen in RiftJudge FAQ #9380 regarding the use of Gust in response to other chain items.

question: Does using Emperor's Divide on a unit that is ready exhaust it?
answer:
No, using Emperor's Divide on a unit that is ready does not exhaust it.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #8882 and FAQ #7964, when a unit is moved by a card effect, its state (Ready or Exhausted) does not change unless the card explicitly states otherwise. Because Emperor's Divide does not contain text instructing you to exhaust the units being moved, they retain their "Ready" status upon arriving at your base.

question: It's my turn and there's an empty battlefield "Sunken Temple". I decided to conquer it, so I move my Noxus Hopeful to it. In my priority, I play a Blood Rush without repeat. I conquer the battlefield, so the question is: can I pay 1 to draw a card by conquering Sunken Temple with a Mighty unit?
answer:
No, you cannot use the effect of Sunken Temple to draw a card in this scenario.

Reasoning

According to RiftJudge FAQ #4146 and #8999, Sunken Temple’s ability is a triggered ability that requires the unit conquering the battlefield to be Mighty (having 5 or more Might) at the exact moment the conquer occurs.

Noxus Hopeful's Might: Noxus Hopeful has a base Might of 4.

Blood Rush Effect: Blood Rush grants the target a Might bonus specifically "while it's an attacker."

Timing and Status: When you move your unit to an empty battlefield to conquer it, your unit is not an attacker; it is simply a unit moving to an empty battlefield. Because your unit is not currently attacking, the Might bonus from Blood Rush is not active, and its Might remains 4.

Failure to Trigger: Because your unit’s Might is only 4 at the moment the conquer is established, the "Mighty" condition on Sunken Temple is not met. Consequently, the ability does not trigger, and you cannot pay the cost to draw a card.

Even if you were to order your actions differently, Sunken Temple checks for the "Mighty" status at the precise moment of the conquer. If the unit is not Mighty at that exact time, the ability fails to trigger entirely, and buffs applied later or from conditional states that are not met do not retroactively satisfy the requirement.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules, as the specific interaction between Blood Rush and the Assault keyword was not explicitly confirmed in the provided documentation.

question: I'm defending at a battlefield, my opponent attacks. He passes priority to me, I play a spell. The spell resolves. Who has priority after my spell resolves?
answer:
To determine who has priority after your spell resolves during a showdown, we follow the established showdown timing flow.

According to FAQ #9365 and FAQ #5067, in a showdown, when you (the defender) play a spell/reaction and it resolves, priority returns to the attacker.

Sequence of Events:

Attacker passes priority: The attacker chooses not to play an action or reaction, passing focus to you.

Defender (You) plays a spell: You play a spell to start a chain (or add to one).

Chain resolves: The spell executes its effects.

Priority returns to the Attacker: Once the chain is empty (or the spell has finished resolving), priority returns to the attacker. They may now choose to play an action, a reaction, or pass priority again.

Important Note: Combat does not resolve until both players pass priority consecutively while the chain is empty. As long as players continue to add items to the chain, the showdown continues. If the attacker passes priority back to you after your spell resolves, and you subsequently pass priority, the showdown will conclude (as per FAQ #8632).

question: Can I have two rune up, one exhausted one ready, can I tap the ready one to ready the exhausted one?
answer:
No, you cannot tap (exhaust) a ready rune to ready an exhausted rune.

According to CR 416.1 and CR 415.1, Ready and Exhaust are states that mark a card's availability. There is no general game rule that allows you to "tap" or exhaust one rune to ready another.

To ready an exhausted rune, you must use a specific card ability or game effect that explicitly instructs you to "ready a rune" or "ready an exhausted rune." For example, some cards may have abilities that trigger or are activated to provide a "ready" effect. If you simply exhaust a rune, it only adds 1 energy to your pool (per Rule 163.2.a), and the rune remains exhausted until your next Beginning Phase (Rule 315.1.b) or until a card effect readies it for you.

question: If I play Fizz to play Ride the Wind on him and move him to BF Abandoned Hall, can I give that Fizz +1 or not, since he wasn't at BF when the spell was played, only when it resolved and moved him?
answer:
No, you cannot give the Fizz, Trickster +1 [M] (Might) from the Abandoned Hall in this scenario.

The Reasoning

The ability of Abandoned Hall is a triggered ability that occurs when a spell is played. Triggered abilities are placed on the chain as soon as the spell is finalized (Rule 359.3). Because Fizz, Trickster's ability is what plays the spell from your trash, the following sequence occurs:

Fizz Enters Play: You play Fizz, Trickster. His "When you play me" ability triggers and is added to the chain.

Fizz's Ability Resolves: You choose Ride the Wind from your trash to play.

Spell Finalized: Ride the Wind is finalized. Because a spell has been played, the Abandoned Hall ability triggers and is added to the chain.

Chain State: The chain now contains the Abandoned Hall trigger.

Targeting: The Abandoned Hall trigger requires you to choose a unit you control at the Abandoned Hall. Because Fizz has not yet been moved by Ride the Wind (which is still pending on the chain), he is not yet at the battlefield and is not a legal target for the Hall's trigger.

Resolution: The Abandoned Hall trigger resolves. Since no eligible unit is present, you cannot grant the +1 [M]. Finally, Ride the Wind resolves, and you move Fizz to the Abandoned Hall.

This interpretation is consistent with RiftJudge FAQ #9723, which confirms that because the trigger condition occurs and is placed on the chain before the unit moves to the battlefield, the unit cannot be a valid target for the effect.

question: If I play Baron to a battlefield and my opponent has an Apathetic Vex, he gets stunned. Does he go back to base?
answer:
No, Baron Nashor does not go back to your base.

Reasoning

Stun Effect: As established by RiftJudge FAQ #9240 and FAQ #8685, Vex, Apathetic's ability is a triggered ability that programmatically selects the unit you just played. Because it is programmatic selection rather than "choosing" or "targeting," it bypasses Baron Nashor's protection ("I can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities").

Stun Mechanics: Being stunned renders a unit "Stunned" (CR 424.1). Stunned units are restricted from contributing might to damage in combat (CR 424.1.b) and gain a restriction against movement for the turn (per the text on Vex, Apathetic).

No Recall: Stunned units remain on the battlefield. There is no game rule or mechanic that causes a unit to automatically return to its base simply for becoming stunned. While combat rules state that attacking units are recalled to base during combat cleanup (Phase 2, step 2 of <showdown_flow>), simply playing a unit (even if it enters an occupied battlefield) does not inherently initiate combat that would result in a recall to base unless a showdown/combat is specifically triggered. Even if combat were triggered, the unit would remain at the battlefield until the combat cleanup step, at which point it would return to base as part of normal combat resolution—not because of the stun itself.

Summary: Your Baron Nashor will remain on the battlefield, stunned and unable to move for the remainder of the turn.

question: Opponent moves his unit on an open Battlefield, attempting to conquer during the showdown. I cast Rengar, Trophy Hunter on this Battlefield. Who is the attacker and defender?
answer:
The Ruling

Attacker: Your opponent (the player who moved their unit to the open battlefield first).

Defender: You (the player who plays Rengar, Trophy Hunter to that same battlefield).

Reasoning

Attacker Designation: According to CR 443.1.a.1 (and confirmed by FAQ #8839, #1485, and #9032), the player who first causes a battlefield to become Contested is designated as the Attacker. When your opponent moved their unit to the empty battlefield, they applied the Contested status, making them the Attacker.

Defender Designation: By playing Rengar, Trophy Hunter to that battlefield while it is already contested by your opponent, you become the Defender (CR 443.1.a.2).

Playing Rengar, Trophy Hunter: Regarding the legality of playing Rengar, Trophy Hunter in this situation: Because your opponent has already moved their unit to the battlefield, there is an enemy unit present. This satisfies the condition for playing the card at that location as a [Reaction] during the ongoing showdown, even though you do not currently have other units there.

Summary of Sequence

Opponent's Move: Your opponent moves a unit to an open battlefield. It becomes Contested and a showdown begins. Your opponent is the Attacker.

Your Response: During the showdown, you play Rengar, Trophy Hunter. Because an enemy unit is present, you may play him to that battlefield as a [Reaction].

Showdown Continues: The showdown proceeds. Because units from both players are now present at the contested battlefield, a combat will begin once the current showdown chain empties and the game returns to a neutral open state.

Combat Designation: When the combat begins, your opponent is officially designated as the Attacker and you are designated as the Defender.

This interpretation is based on the rules for Contested status (CR 447/446), the definitions of Attacker/Defender designations (CR 443.1.a), and the specific card text of Rengar, Trophy Hunter.

Note: I could not fully verify the specific card text for Rengar, Trophy Hunter against the retrieved rules.

question: If I deathgrip my unit which has guardian angel attached, can I still give the might to another unit? Or won't this work because it has been saved by guardian angel?
answer:
No, you cannot give the Might bonus to another unit if you save the first unit using Guardian Angel.

This is because the Might bonus provided by Deathgrip is contingent on the successful completion of the "Kill a friendly unit" instruction. Because Guardian Angel is a replacement effect (Rule 366), it replaces the "die" event with a "heal, exhaust, and recall" event.

Sequence of Events

Play Deathgrip: You target a friendly unit to be killed and another friendly unit to receive the Might bonus.

Resolution: As Deathgrip resolves, it attempts to kill the target unit.

Replacement: Guardian Angel triggers as a replacement effect, replacing the death event with a recall to your base.

Condition Check: Because the unit was not actually killed (the death was prevented), the "If you do" condition for the Might bonus is not met.

Finalization: The Might bonus is not applied. However, you still draw 1 card, as the card draw is not contingent on the kill.

This interaction is consistent with the established rules for replacement effects preventing the specific condition required for a subsequent effect to trigger or resolve.

question: Can you play Cull the Weak in combat if it's not an action or reaction?
answer:
No, you cannot play Cull the Weak during combat.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ (ID 8041), spells that are neither [Action] nor [Reaction] (often referred to as "Main" timing spells) can only be played during your Main Phase, out of a showdown, when the chain is empty.

Why you cannot play it in combat:

Timing Restriction: Combat is a "Showdown State" (Rule 343.1). During a Showdown State, cards that are not [Action] or [Reaction] cannot be played.

Missing Keywords: Cull the Weak does not have the [Action] or [Reaction] keyword, which are the only permissions that allow a card to be played during a showdown or when the chain is not empty.

Spell Category: Because it lacks these keywords, it is restricted to your Main Phase when the board state is "Neutral" (no combat/showdown) and the chain is empty.

While you do not need to control a unit to play Cull the Weak (as it does not target and follows the "do as much as you can" principle), you must always respect the timing permissions of the card itself.

question: For Rek'Sai legend do you have to pay the cost to play the unit that was revealed from the legend ability?
answer:
Yes, you must pay the full cost of the unit when using the Rek'Sai (Void Burrower) legend ability.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9215 and FAQ #284, you are required to pay the card's energy and power costs as normal when you play it using this ability. Only effects that explicitly state "ignoring its cost" allow you to play cards for free.

question: Does an opponent's Vex Apathetic at a Battlefield stun / not allow units to move apply to Reflection unit tokens created from spells like Mirror Image or LeBlanc Legend ability?
answer:
Yes, an opponent's Vex, Apathetic at a battlefield will stun and restrict the movement of Reflection tokens created by Mirror Image and LeBlanc's (Deceiver) ability.

Reasoning

Trigger Condition: Vex, Apathetic has the ability: "When an opponent plays a unit while I'm at a battlefield, [Stun] it. They can't move it this turn."

Playing a Unit: As established in RiftJudge FAQ #8758 and #9485, a unit token is considered "played" if the card effect that creates it explicitly uses the word "play."

Mirror Image states: "Play a ready Reflection unit token to your base."

LeBlanc's (Deceiver) ability states: "...play a ready Reflection unit token there."

Interaction: Because these effects explicitly use the word "play," they satisfy the trigger condition for Vex, Apathetic. When the token enters the board, Vex's triggered ability activates, stunning the token and applying the restriction that it cannot move for the rest of the turn.

As confirmed in RiftJudge FAQ #9240 and #9751, this ability triggers regardless of where on the board the unit is played, provided Vex is at a battlefield.

question: Does Fiora Victorious become mighty when played on Trifarian War Camp?
answer:
No, Fiora, Victorious does not "become Mighty" when played directly onto Trifarian War Camp.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #5835 and #9442:

Trifarian War Camp has a passive ability that grants +1 Might to units at that location.

When you play a unit (such as Fiora, Victorious) directly onto Trifarian War Camp, the +1 Might bonus is applied immediately as the unit enters the battlefield.

Because the bonus is applied instantly upon entry, there is no moment where the unit exists on the battlefield with its base Might before becoming 5 Might; it is 5 Might the instant it arrives.

As defined in Rule 709, a unit "becomes Mighty" only at the moment its Might changes from less than 5 to 5 or greater while it is already a game object in play. Since Fiora is already 5 Might the moment she enters the battlefield, she does not "become Mighty" while on the battlefield, and therefore does not trigger abilities that specifically care about that event.

question: I use Baited Hook to kill a unit, does the unit's Deathknell ability trigger first or can I choose to do the Baited Hook 5 card reveal to play a unit first?
answer:
According to RiftJudge FAQ #8567, when you use Baited Hook to kill a unit with Deathknell, the resolution order is fixed by the rules of the chain (LIFO - Last In, First Out). You do not have a choice to resolve the reveal effect before the Deathknell trigger.

Sequence of Resolution

Activation: You activate Baited Hook by paying its cost and targeting a friendly unit.

Resolution Begins: Baited Hook's effect begins to resolve. It kills the target unit.

Deathknell Triggered: Because the unit has Deathknell, its trigger becomes a "pending item" on the chain. Per CR 429.1.a.1.b and Rule 808.1.d.2, the Deathknell trigger is added to the chain before the Kill instruction is completed.

Baited Hook Continues: Baited Hook continues resolving its remaining instructions (looking at the top 5 cards and playing a new unit).

New Unit Finalizes: Any unit played via Baited Hook enters the board and finalizes immediately. If that new unit has a "When you play me" (WYPM) ability, it is added to the chain as a pending item.

Resolution (LIFO): The chain resolves in reverse order:

Any WYPM ability from the new unit resolves first.

The Deathknell trigger resolves last.

In summary: You do not choose the order. The Deathknell trigger is created first, but because the chain resolves in LIFO order, the Deathknell trigger will always resolve after the effects of the Baited Hook have finished.

question: I played Promising Future. My opponent played Relentless Pursuit to try and move into a battlefield. Does the showdown go through before I can do my 5 cards from Promising Future?
answer:
No, the showdown does not happen before you finish playing your cards from Promising Future.

According to the official rulings for Promising Future, all cards revealed and played during its resolution must be fully played and resolved before any showdown or combat begins.

Here is how the timing works:

Resolution of Promising Future: When you play Promising Future, it begins to resolve. Both players look at their cards, banish one, and then, starting with the next player, play their chosen cards one by one.

No Interruption: These cards are played as part of the resolution of Promising Future. Because a spell's resolution cannot be interrupted, your opponent cannot play Relentless Pursuit (which is an [Action] or [Reaction] card) to move a unit and start a showdown until Promising Future has finished resolving completely.

Showdown Staging: If the cards played via Promising Future trigger a showdown (for example, by moving a unit to a battlefield that becomes contested), that showdown is "staged." It will only actually start once the chain is empty and the turn returns to an Open State after Promising Future and all its associated card plays have completely finished resolving.

In summary, Promising Future must fully resolve first. Only after the chain is empty and the board state is finalized will any potential showdowns begin. Your opponent cannot interrupt your card plays to force a showdown before you finish.

question: When Irresistable Faefolk moves to an unoccupied battlefield and uses its effect to move an enemy unit to that battlefield, who is the attacker and defender?
answer:
When you move Irresistible Faefolk to an unoccupied (uncontrolled) battlefield and use its ability to move an enemy unit to that same battlefield, you are the attacker and the enemy unit is the defender.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9581, #9665, and #9714, the determination of attacker and defender designations is based on which player applied the "Contested" status to the battlefield first (CR 461.2.b.1).

Sequence of Events

Move: You move Irresistible Faefolk to an unoccupied battlefield. This applies the "Contested" status to that battlefield. Because you are the player who applied this status, you gain the Attacker designation.

Trigger: Irresistible Faefolk's ability ("When I move to a battlefield...") triggers. You place this ability on the chain.

Resolution: When the ability resolves, you move an enemy unit to that same battlefield.

Combat: Because units from opposing players are now present, the showdown transitions into a Combat Showdown.

Because you were the one who applied the "Contested" status to the battlefield first, you remain the attacker, and your opponent's unit is the defender, even though your ability was the one that moved their unit into the combat.

question: Do I need my own equipment on the field to play Acceptable Losses?
answer:
No, you do not need to control your own gear on the field to play Acceptable Losses.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #4344 and #9554, you can play Acceptable Losses even if you do not control any gear, as long as your opponent does. The card does not target, and at resolution, each player who controls gear will choose one to kill.

question: Do cards with hidden only gain reaction speed when they are played facedown or can they also be played at reaction speed from hand?
answer:
Cards with the Hidden keyword can only be played at Reaction speed after they have been hidden facedown on a battlefield. They cannot be played at Reaction speed directly from your hand.

According to Rule 811.1.b, the Hidden keyword functions as follows:

"While this card is in your hand or in your Champion Zone on your turn during an Open State, you may pay [A] to hide this facedown at a battlefield you control... Beginning on the next turn, this gains [Reaction] and you may play this, ignoring its base cost."

To summarize:

From your hand: The card must first be played using the "Hide" action (which costs [A]) to place it facedown on a battlefield. This action is performed during an Open State on your turn.

From the battlefield (facedown): Beginning on the next turn after it was hidden, the card gains the Reaction keyword, which allows you to play it at Reaction speed.

Essentially, Hidden is a setup mechanic that requires you to place the card on the board before it gains the ability to be played at Reaction speed on a later turn.

question: Does Rek'Sai give units Accelerate free or do you have to pay for them?
answer:
No, Rek'Sai, Breacher does not make the Accelerate cost free; you must still pay for it if you want the unit to enter the board ready.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9737 and CR 805.1.b, Accelerate is an optional additional cost of [1] Energy and 1 Power. Rek'Sai, Breacher’s ability grants the keyword to your units played from outside your hand, which gives you the option to pay that cost.

Here is how the interaction works:

Optional Cost: You are not required to pay the cost. If you choose not to, the unit will enter the battlefield exhausted (the default state).

Payment Timing: If you want the unit to enter the board ready, you must pay the [1] Energy and 1 Power during the "Pay Costs" step of playing that unit.

Tokens: This applies to tokens as well. As noted in RiftJudge FAQ #9360, when an ability plays a token, Rek'Sai, Breacher grants it Accelerate, and you may pay the cost as part of the process of playing that token to have it enter ready.

question: How many times can you repeat?
answer:
You can pay the Repeat cost once per instance of the Repeat keyword on a card.

According to Rule 820.1.c.3, each individual Repeat cost can be paid only a single time. However, if a card has multiple instances of the Repeat keyword (either printed on the card or granted by another effect), you may pay for each instance individually.

For each instance of Repeat that you pay for:

The spell's instructions are executed an additional time (Rule 820.3).

The spell is only "played" once, regardless of how many times its instructions are executed (Rule 820.3.a).

As confirmed by RiftJudge FAQ #8328 and #9252, you must decide whether to pay for each available Repeat cost at the time you play the spell from your hand. You cannot add Repeats retroactively after the spell is on the chain.

question: Do unit tokens count as units played?
answer:
Yes, playing a token unit counts as playing a unit.

According to Rule 350.2, while tokens are not cards, they can still be played. Rule 182.1.a states that tokens are played by their owner following all applicable steps for playing a card (or unit). Additionally, RiftJudge FAQ #9440 confirms that playing a token unit counts as playing a unit.

question: Does Skyfall of Areion make Yone Blademaster ability trigger on holds?
answer:
No, Skyfall of Areion does not cause Yone, Blademaster's ability to trigger on every "Hold" action.

1. Skyfall of Areion's Function

According to FAQ #5622 and #288, Skyfall of Areion modifies the equipped unit's triggered abilities, allowing "When I conquer..." effects to trigger on both Conquer and Hold scoring, and "When I hold..." effects to trigger on both. It only modifies the equipped unit's abilities and does not change the fundamental definitions of the "Hold" or "Conquer" actions, nor does it override the specific conditions (such as "uncontrolled") within a unit's ability text.

2. Yone, Blademaster's Condition

Yone, Blademaster’s ability requires: "When I conquer a battlefield that was uncontrolled..."
A standard Hold action is defined as maintaining control of a battlefield you already control (CR 466.2). Because you already control the battlefield during a standard Hold, the condition that the battlefield was "uncontrolled" immediately prior to the action cannot be met. Consequently, Skyfall alone does not satisfy Yone's "uncontrolled" requirement.

3. The Exception: Reckoner's Arena

The confusion regarding this interaction stems from specific FAQs (#9342, #9002) involving Reckoner's Arena.

Reckoner's Arena has the unique ability: "When you hold here, activate the conquer effects of units here."

This battlefield effect acts as a bridge: it forces the "When I conquer" abilities of units present to trigger during a "Hold" action.

It is this unique battlefield ability that creates the window where Yone’s ability can trigger during a Hold. Even then, the "uncontrolled" condition must still be satisfied.

Summary

Does Skyfall make Yone trigger on all Holds? No.

Does Skyfall make Yone trigger on all Conquers? Yes, because Yone is a conquer-based effect and Skyfall enables that.

When does Yone trigger on a Hold? Only when an external game effect (like Reckoner's Arena) specifically forces a "Conquer" trigger to fire during a "Hold" action, and the specific condition of that unit's ability (e.g., "uncontrolled") is independently met.

Note: I could not fully verify the interaction between the 'uncontrolled' condition and the Hold action against the retrieved rules.

question: Can I deathgrip a unit and save it with Sett legend power?
answer:
Yes, you can use Sett's legend ability to save a unit targeted by Deathgrip, but the Might bonus will not be applied to the second unit.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9246, this interaction works as follows:

Playing Deathgrip: You play Deathgrip targeting a buffed friendly unit.

Resolution: As Deathgrip resolves, it attempts to execute its "Kill a friendly unit" instruction.

Replacement: Because the unit is buffed and would die, Sett's ability (a replacement effect) triggers to intervene. You pay the cost (exhaust Sett and pay [C]), and the unit is recalled to your base instead of being killed.

Condition Check: Because the replacement effect prevents the unit from actually dying, the "If you do" condition for the Might bonus in Deathgrip is not met. Therefore, you do not give the Might bonus to another unit.

Finalization: You still draw 1 card, as the card draw is not contingent on the kill.

Important Nuances:

Replacement, Not Trigger: Sett's ability is a replacement effect, not a triggered ability. It modifies the event as it happens and does not use the chain.

Buff Spent: As part of the cost for Sett's ability, the buff on the unit is spent (removed).

Identity: Because the unit is recalled to your base rather than sent to the trash, it does not "die," so any "Deathknell" abilities the unit may have had will not trigger.

question: Can my opponent attack and play an action, and can I respond with an action?
answer:
No, you cannot respond to an Action spell with another Action spell.

When your opponent plays an Action spell, they start a Closed State (a chain). Once a chain is open and has items on it, you may only play cards or abilities with the [Reaction] keyword to respond.

According to Riftbound mechanics:

[Action] cards can only be played when the state is Open (no chain exists).

[Reaction] cards can be played in both Open and Closed states.

Sequence:

Your opponent plays an Action spell, starting a chain. The state is now Closed.

You cannot play an Action spell because the state is Closed. You may only play a [Reaction] card.

Once the chain fully resolves (including any Reactions that were added), the state becomes Open again.

Only then, when focus passes back to you, can you play an Action spell.

This is consistent with several RiftJudge FAQs, including FAQ #1787 and #2818, which clarify that players can only respond to Actions with Reactions, and must wait for the chain to resolve before they can play an Action themselves.

question: Does Vex - Apathetic counter Lillia's ready sprites?
answer:
No, Vex, Apathetic does not counter the Sprite token created by Lillia, Fae Fawn's ability, but it will interact with it.

Explanation

To clarify the interaction:

Lillia's Ability: When Lillia moves, her ability plays a 3 [M] Sprite token. Because Lillia's ability uses the word "play," it fulfills the trigger condition for Vex, Apathetic ("When an opponent plays a unit...").

Interaction: As established in RiftJudge FAQ #8758 and RiftJudge FAQ #9485, tokens created by card effects that use the word "play" trigger Vex's ability.

Result: When the Sprite token enters the battlefield, Vex's triggered ability will resolve. The Sprite token will be Stunned and will gain the restriction that it cannot move for the remainder of the turn.

Why it is not a "Counter"

In Riftbound, Countering (CR 426) specifically refers to negating the playing of a card or the activation of an ability, which clears that item from the chain and prevents it from doing anything.

Vex's ability does not Counter Lillia's ability or the playing of the token; instead, it waits for the token to enter the battlefield and then applies a Stun effect to that unit. The Sprite token still successfully enters play, but it arrives in a Stunned state.

question: If I conquer as a Rek'sai player the battlefield The Candlelit Sanctum, what effect will be first on the chain? Or can I choose if I want to trigger the battlefield's effect or my champion Rek'sai conquer effect first?
answer:
Because you control both the battlefield's effect and the ability triggered by your conquer, you get to choose the order.

According to Rule 383.3.d and clarified in RiftJudge FAQ #7191:

When multiple triggered abilities you control are triggered simultaneously (such as a unit’s "When I conquer" effect and a battlefield’s "When you conquer" effect), you as the controller choose the order in which they are placed on the chain.

Once you place them on the chain, opponents can then add reactions to that chain before the triggers resolve.

The triggers will resolve in reverse order (Last In, First Out).

How to sequence this:

Conquer: The showdown concludes, and you conquer The Candlelit Sanctum.

Declare Order: Since both effects trigger simultaneously, you declare the order. If you say "Chain 1: Rek'Sai's effect, Chain 2: Candlelit Sanctum's effect," then Sanctum resolves first.

Resolve: The items on the chain resolve one by one according to your chosen order.

Note: While you mentioned "Rek'Sai's conquer effect," please verify the exact text on your version of Rek'Sai. The version of Rek'Sai retrieved (Rek'Sai, Breacher) does not have a "When I conquer" ability. If you are using a different version or a legend ability associated with Rek'Sai, the same logic above applies: if you control both triggers, you order them.

question: Can I react to Lonely Poro Deathknell trigger with an Ambush unit to send it to the battlefield and still draw the card from the Poro?
answer:
Yes, you can play an Ambush unit while a Lonely Poro's Deathknell trigger is on the chain, and you will still draw the card.

The Ruling

You will draw the card from Lonely Poro's Deathknell because the "alone" condition is checked at the moment of death, not when the trigger resolves. Since the Lonely Poro met the criteria of being "alone" when it died, its Deathknell trigger is valid and will resolve successfully, regardless of whether you play a new unit to the battlefield later in the chain.

Why this works

"Alone" is a Historical Check: According to FAQ #373 and Rule 808.1.d.3, Lonely Poro's "alone" condition is satisfied if there were no other friendly units at that location at the moment of death. Once the Deathknell trigger is created and added to the chain, it retains the information that the condition was met.

Chain Resolution (LIFO): Per Rule 326.1 and Rule 359.3, the chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out order. Even if you play an Ambush unit as a reaction to the Deathknell trigger, the unit enters the battlefield before the Deathknell trigger resolves. Because the "alone" condition was already locked in at the moment of death, the arrival of this new unit does not retroactively invalidate the Deathknell.

Sequence of Resolution

Death Event: Lonely Poro dies while "alone" (no other friendly units at its location). The Deathknell trigger is created and added to the chain.

Reaction: You play an Ambush unit in response to the Deathknell trigger, adding it to the chain.

Resolution: The chain resolves (LIFO).

First, the Ambush unit enters the battlefield.

Second, the Lonely Poro's Deathknell trigger resolves. Because the condition was satisfied at the time of death, you draw your card.

Summary: Your Ambush unit arriving at the battlefield does not invalidate the Deathknell because the "alone" check is based on the state of the board at the time of the Lonely Poro's death, not the state of the board when the trigger resolves.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: Can I react to Watcher ability?
answer:
Yes, you can react to the Thousand-Tailed Watcher's "When you play me" ability.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #93 and FAQ #5127, the Thousand-Tailed Watcher has a "When you play me" triggered ability that uses the chain, and players may respond to it using [Reaction] cards.

How the timing works:

Playing the Unit: When you play Thousand-Tailed Watcher, it enters the board. This does not create a chain and cannot be reacted to (per Rule 3722/7617).

Triggered Ability: Once the Watcher is on the board, its "When you play me" ability triggers and is placed on the chain.

Reacting: Because the ability is now on the chain, players can play [Reaction] cards.

Per CR 407.4, other players have an opportunity to play Reactions before the resolution of spells and abilities on the chain.

Following the Showdown Timing Flowchart, if this occurs during a Showdown, the chain resolves in reverse order (LIFO - Last In, First Out).

Important Notes:

No Actions: You can only use [Reaction] cards to respond to this trigger; you cannot play [Action] cards.

Effective Timing: As noted in RiftJudge FAQ #2236, if you play a unit as a reaction to the Watcher's trigger, your new unit will be on the field when the chain resolves, meaning it will be affected by the Watcher's ability. If you play the unit after the trigger has already finished resolving, it will not be affected.

question: Can I use Charm to move an enemy unit at a battlefield to a battlefield I control?
answer:
Yes, you can use Charm to move an enemy unit from one battlefield to a battlefield you control.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #7385, you can use Charm to move an enemy unit from anywhere on the board (including from another battlefield) to a battlefield you occupy. This movement is not restricted by standard movement rules (like the Ganking keyword), as Charm is a card effect and not a Standard Move.

Furthermore, if you move the enemy unit to a battlefield you occupy, this will force a showdown, and the opponent who controls the unit you moved will become the attacker in that showdown.

question: If I control Vex, Cheerless in combat and my opponent is at 6 points, can I play Find Your Center for free?
answer:
Ruling: Yes. Both Vex, Cheerless's discount and Find Your Center's conditional discount apply to the total cost of the spell, not to a specific component. You may apply them in any order you choose.

Sequence:

Start with Find Your Center's base cost of [3] Energy

Apply Vex, Cheerless's discount: reduce by [1] Energy to [2] Energy

Apply Find Your Center's discount (opponent within 3 points of Victory Score): reduce by [2] Energy to [0] Energy

Nuances:

When multiple discounts apply to the total cost (rather than to specific components), you may order them as you like to minimize the final cost.

This only works when Vex is YOUR card; if Vex belonged to your opponent, it would increase the cost instead of decreasing it.

question: If my opponent plays Cull the Weak with Repeat and I only have a single unit with a Guardian Angel equipped, does the unit die?
answer:
Ruling: Yes, your unit will die. Cull the Weak with Repeat creates two separate instances of "Each player kills one of their units." The first instance triggers Guardian Angel's replacement effect, which kills the Guardian Angel instead, then heals, exhausts, and recalls your unit to your base. However, when the second instance resolves, your unit is still a valid target because Cull the Weak does not restrict the kill instruction to units at a battlefield—units at your base are still on the board and can be chosen. Since Guardian Angel was already destroyed by the first instance, your unit must be killed by the second instance.

Sequence:

First instance resolves: Guardian Angel replacement effect triggers, Guardian Angel is killed, unit is healed/exhausted/recalled to base

Second instance resolves: You must choose a unit to kill; your unit at base is still a valid choice and dies

Nuances:

Guardian Angel is a one-time use replacement effect that is destroyed when it saves the unit

Units at your base are still "on the board" and can be targeted by effects that don't specify battlefield location

question: When assigning combat damage to multiple defending units, must I assign lethal damage to each unit before assigning damage to another?
answer:
Ruling: No. The only mandatory restriction for combat damage assignment is the Tank keyword—you must assign lethal damage to Tank units before assigning to non-Tank units. Beyond that, you can choose how to distribute your remaining damage among defending units and are not required to assign lethal damage to each unit before assigning damage to others.

Sequence:

Assign lethal damage to all Tank units first

Distribute remaining damage among other defending units as you choose

Nuances:

If you have 4 Might attacking into a 5 Might and 3 Might defender (no Tanks), you can assign all 4 damage to the 5 Might unit, leaving the 3 Might unit undamaged.

After satisfying Tank requirements, you can assign partial damage to one unit even if another unit could be killed with that damage.

The lethal damage rule prevents overkilling a unit before moving to another, but does not mandate killing every possible target.

question: When a defending unit survives at the battlefield where it was attacked and the attacker is still alive, what happens?
answer:
According to the Riftbound core rules and the established FAQs, if both the attacking and defending units remain at a battlefield after the combat damage step, the attacking units are recalled to their base.

According to CR 463.1.a.2 and FAQ 5531:

Combat Resolution: After damage is dealt, if both players still have surviving units at the battlefield, the attacking units are recalled to base.

Control: The defender retains control of the battlefield, as the attackers have been recalled and no conquest has occurred.

Recall Nuance: Per FAQ 6909, this recall does not count as a "move," so move-related triggers will not fire. Additionally, units recalled in this manner remain exhausted if they were exhausted when they entered the showdown.
