question: If I have scored on both battlefields this turn, move off my units and then move a unit onto the battlefield, does a showdown start?
answer:
Yes, a showdown does start when you move a unit onto that battlefield, even if you have already scored on both battlefields this turn.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10027 and Rule 344, a showdown occurs whenever a battlefield becomes contested, regardless of whether it has already been scored that turn.

Here is the breakdown of why this happens:

Losing Control: When you move your last unit out of the battlefield to your base, the battlefield becomes unoccupied and uncontrolled (CR 323.5).

Contesting: When you move a unit back into that battlefield, you are moving into a location that you do not currently control. This makes the battlefield Contested (CR 447).

Showdown Trigger: Because the battlefield is contested and the turn is in a neutral open state, a showdown begins (Rule 344).

Important Nuances:

No Scoring: You will not score another holding point or trigger conquering effects (such as from specific cards) at that battlefield for the rest of the turn, because you have already scored it earlier (CR 467, FAQ #7447).

Non-Combat: Because the battlefield was unoccupied when the showdown began, this will be a non-combat showdown (unless your opponent also moves a unit there simultaneously, creating a combat scenario). Per Rule 348.2.a, since you are the only player with units present, you will regain control of the battlefield once the showdown closes.

question: Does Deathgrip draw if target unit is removed?
answer:
Yes, you will still draw one card.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10082, #10334, and #10055, the draw effect of Deathgrip is not contingent on the success of the kill or the Might bonus.

Why this happens:

Partial Resolution: When you play Deathgrip, you must target two friendly units (one to kill and one to receive Might). If one of these units is removed (e.g., via Gust) before Deathgrip resolves, the spell still attempts to resolve as much as possible (Rule 359.3.e.11).

Target Legality: If the unit targeted to be killed remains on the board, it is destroyed as instructed. Even if the unit targeted to receive the Might bonus is removed and the bonus cannot be applied, the spell continues to resolve.

The Draw: Because the "Draw 1" instruction is not linked to the success of the kill or the Might bonus, it is performed regardless of whether those previous instructions successfully executed or were rendered impossible due to mistargeting.

Summary: As long as the spell itself was played legally (by having two valid targets at the moment it was placed on the chain), you will draw one card when it resolves, even if the targets leave the board in the meantime.

question: Can I play Rengar bouncing when my opponent is conquering and I have no units there?
answer:
To answer your question, no, you cannot play Rengar, Pouncing to a battlefield your opponent is currently conquering if you have no units there.

Reasoning:

Placement Restrictions: According to his card text and supporting RiftJudge FAQs (specifically FAQ #9634 and FAQ #427), Rengar can only be played to:

Your base.

A battlefield you control.

A battlefield you are currently attacking.

Definition of Attacking: Simply contesting a battlefield (or defending against an opponent who is in the process of conquering it) does not grant you the "attacker" designation. Because you are not the player who initiated the move to that battlefield, you do not meet the "attacking" criteria required to play Rengar there.

No Units Present: Since you have no units at that battlefield and do not control it, you have no legal location to place him at that specific battlefield.

Summary: Unless you already control the battlefield or were the player who initiated the attack on it, Rengar's specific play restriction cannot be satisfied. You could, however, play him to your base or to another battlefield you currently control, provided you have the necessary energy.

question: If I void assault targeting my Yone and the enemies Rengar, moving Rengar to base and Yone to the battlefield Rengar was at, does Yone's passive trigger off Conqueror?
answer:
Yes, Yone, Blademaster's ability will trigger in this scenario.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10336, moving Yone into a battlefield and simultaneously moving the only enemy unit out results in that battlefield becoming uncontrolled during the cleanup phase (before the showdown begins). When Yone then conquers this now-uncontrolled battlefield during the resulting showdown, his ability will trigger.

Sequence of Events:

Void Assault: You play Void Assault, moving Yone to the battlefield and Rengar to the base.

State Change: The battlefield becomes contested.

Cleanup Phase: During cleanup, because there are no enemy units there and no showdown is currently ongoing, the opponent loses control per Rule 187.4.c. The battlefield becomes uncontrolled.

Showdown: A non-combat showdown opens, and Yone conquers the now-uncontrolled battlefield.

Trigger: Because Yone conquered a battlefield that was uncontrolled, his ability triggers and is placed on the chain.

This is my interpretation based on the official FAQs regarding Yone's conquer ability and Void Assault. No official FAQ exists for this specific unit interaction beyond the established logic for how Yone and Void Assault interact with battlefield control.

question: When an ability instructs you to play a card from a zone other than your hand, do you have to pay its cost?
answer:
Ruling: Yes, you must pay the full cost of the card unless the ability explicitly states otherwise. Riftbound uses the principle that costs must be paid when playing cards, and only abilities that include phrases like "ignoring its cost" or "play it for [cost]" allow you to bypass the normal cost.

Nuances:

This applies to abilities like Rek'Sai, Swarm Queen's "When I attack" ability that instructs you to play a card from the top of your deck.

Any mandatory additional costs (such as those from keywords or passive abilities) would still apply even if the base cost were ignored.

question: If I play Flurry of Blades before Dazzling Aurora triggers, then reveal Elder Dragon from Aurora and the opponent plays Star-Crossed in response, do all enemy units die from the 1 damage?
answer:
Ruling: Yes, all enemy units with 1 damage from Flurry of Blades will die before the opponent can play Star-Crossed. Elder Dragon's passive ability becomes active immediately when it enters the battlefield, making the 1 damage lethal during the mandatory cleanup that occurs before the "When you play me" trigger is finalized.

Sequence:

Flurry of Blades resolves, dealing 1 damage to all units (damage remains marked)

Dazzling Aurora triggers and Elder Dragon is played to the battlefield

Elder Dragon enters play and its passive ability becomes active immediately

A cleanup is queued as an outstanding task

The HOT FEPR system pauses the chain to handle the cleanup before the "When you play me" trigger can be finalized

During cleanup, the 1 damage on enemy units is now lethal due to Elder Dragon's passive, destroying them

After cleanup completes, the "When you play me" trigger is finalized and players receive priority

At this point Star-Crossed could be played, but the enemy units are already destroyed

Nuances:

Passive abilities become active immediately when a permanent enters the battlefield

Outstanding tasks (like cleanup) must be handled before the FEPR process continues with pending triggers

question: If I play an Irresistible Faefolk to an occupied battlefield and move an enemy unit from base to that battlefield, am I then the attacker still or do I become the defender?
answer:
When you move Irresistible Faefolk to a battlefield that is already occupied by an opponent's unit, the battlefield is already contested (or becomes contested by the arrival of your unit).

According to CR 461.2.b.1 and the established RiftJudge FAQs regarding this specific card, the determination of attacker and defender designations is based on which player applied the "Contested" status to the battlefield first.

If the battlefield was already contested by your opponent: Your opponent is already the attacker. By moving your unit (and subsequently pulling another enemy unit) to that battlefield, you do not change the attacker/defender designations; your opponent remains the attacker and you are the defender.

If the battlefield was NOT already contested: By moving your unit to an occupied battlefield, you are the one who applies the "Contested" status. In this scenario, you are the attacker and the units already present (and the one you moved) are the defenders.

Summary

If your opponent was already the attacker because they contested that battlefield first, moving an Irresistible Faefolk there does not change their status. You remain the defender.

If you are the one applying the "Contested" status (e.g., you move to an uncontested battlefield, or you are the first player to move into a battlefield that was previously empty), you are the attacker.

This interpretation is supported by RiftJudge FAQ #9423 and #10794, which clarify that if you move into a battlefield already contested by your opponent, they remain the attacker regardless of your unit's movement ability.

question: If I have a 4 might unit defending at the Frozen Fortress and my opponent plays a Thousand Tail Watcher dealing the -3 might to a minimum of -1, does my unit die?
answer:
Yes, your unit will die.

Here is the breakdown of why this happens based on the Riftbound rules:

Sequence of Events

Thousand-Tailed Watcher: When your opponent plays this unit, its ability triggers, giving your unit -3 Might. Your unit's Might is reduced from 4 to 1 (as per the "minimum of 1" clause).

Frozen Fortress: This battlefield's ability reads: "At the start of each player's Beginning Phase, deal 1 to each unit here."

If your unit is at the Frozen Fortress battlefield, it has 1 damage marked on it from the battlefield's ability.

Lethal Damage Check: According to CR 143.2.b, a unit is killed if it has non-zero damage marked on it that is equal to or greater than its current Might.

Your unit now has 1 Might and 1 damage marked on it.

Since the marked damage (1) equals its current Might (1), the unit is killed during the cleanup check.

Key Rules

Might vs. Damage: Damage is "marked" on units (Rule 143.3) and does not reduce Might directly. The unit dies during the cleanup check when damage equals or exceeds Might (RiftJudge FAQ #91, #2141).

Minimum Might: As confirmed by RiftJudge FAQ #91, the "minimum of 1 Might" clause on Thousand-Tailed Watcher only prevents the Might reduction itself from going lower, but it does not protect the unit from death if the damage marked on the unit (from Frozen Fortress) meets or exceeds that new Might value.

question: If I react to a charm by playing an Ambush Rengar which immediately resolves, will my opponent then have a window after that to react to their own charm on the chain?
answer:
Yes, your opponent will have an opportunity to react to their own Charm after your Rengar, Trophy Hunter has finished entering play.

Here is the breakdown of how this interaction proceeds:

Chain State: When you play Rengar, Trophy Hunter as a [Reaction] to Charm, the chain is in a "Closed State" (it contains the Charm spell).

Playing the Permanent: You follow the process of playing a card. Once you finish finalizing Rengar, he is no longer "Pending" (Rule 359.1).

Entering Play: Per Rule 359.2, as a Permanent, Rengar leaves the chain and becomes a game object. He enters the board at the chosen location (exhausted) (Rule 359.2.c).

Priority/Reaction Window: According to RiftJudge FAQ #2028, as soon as a permanent (a unit or gear) resolves and enters play, the player who controls the next item on the chain (in this case, your opponent, who controls the Charm spell) gains priority.

This gives your opponent an opportunity to add a new [Reaction] to the chain, or simply allow the chain to continue resolving.

If they pass, you would then receive priority, and so on, until both players pass in sequence.

Resolution: Only after both players have passed priority consecutively without adding anything new to the chain does the topmost item (the Charm spell) resolve.

Summary: Your opponent does not lose their chance to react to their own spell. Once your unit has entered play, the priority system resumes, and all players retain the standard opportunity to add reactions to the chain before the next spell on the chain resolves.

question: I am using Master Yi Wuju Master Legend. When I defend with Fiora Peerless, do I get the +2 from Yi first, then my Fiora ability procs going to 10 might, or does it do the double before and then apply the +2 might?
answer:
When defending with Fiora, Peerless while your Master Yi, Wuju Bladesman legend is active (and Fiora is defending alone), your Fiora will reach a total of 10 Might.

The calculation follows the game's layering and ability types:

Sequence of Events

Passive Application: Master Yi's bonus is a passive ability (it does not use the chain). As soon as the showdown begins and Fiora is designated as the lone defender, her base might of 3 receives the +2 bonus from Master Yi, resulting in 5 Might.

Triggered Ability: Fiora's "When I defend" ability is a triggered ability. It is placed onto the Initial Chain.

Resolution: When the Fiora trigger resolves from the chain, it doubles her current might. Since her current might is 5, it doubles to 10.

Why it works this way

Layering: Passive bonuses that modify stats (like Master Yi's +2) are applied in the Arithmetic layer. Because Fiora's trigger is a "When" ability, it acts upon her current value at the time of resolution.

Passive vs. Triggered: As confirmed in RiftJudge FAQ #9025, Master Yi's bonus is a continuous passive, not a trigger. It does not wait for a chain to resolve; it is active immediately upon the condition being met. Fiora's ability, however, is a trigger that doubles the current might. Since the +2 is already applied when her trigger resolves, the math correctly results in (3 + 2) × 2 = 10.

This interpretation is based on the constant application of passive abilities and the standard resolution order of the Initial Chain as defined in the Showdown Flow.

question: If I use Heedless as the attacker, can I play a unit to the battlefield I was attacking?
answer:
As the attacker, no, you cannot play the resurrected unit to the battlefield you are attacking.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9753 and the related ruling logic:

Battlefield Control: During a showdown, you do not control the contested battlefield. Because you are the attacker, your control is restricted to your own base (and potentially other battlefields you occupy), but you cannot play units into the battlefield you are currently attacking.

Heedless Resurrection's Restrictions: While Heedless Resurrection creates a chain that allows you to play a unit from your trash, that unit must be played to a valid location. As the attacker, the contested battlefield is not a valid destination for you to play a unit.

Summary of the interaction:

You initiate the Heedless Resurrection chain as a [Reaction].

You pay the cost (killing a friendly unit).

Even though Heedless Resurrection is on the chain (keeping the game state closed), you still cannot play the resurrected unit into the battlefield you are attacking, because as the attacker, you lack the required control of that battlefield to place a unit there.

question: If I use Imperial Decree and Bellows Breath on an Irelia with Guardian Angel, will both die?
answer:
Yes, your Irelia will be killed.

The interaction between Imperial Decree and a Repeated spell results in multiple kill triggers. Because Guardian Angel is a one-time replacement effect, it can only save the unit from the first kill trigger; the subsequent trigger will then find and kill the unit.

Sequence of Events:

Imperial Decree is played and resolves, creating an active effect for the turn.

Bellows Breath is played with the [Repeat] cost paid, targeting Irelia.

Bellows Breath resolves:

The first instance deals 1 damage. Imperial Decree triggers, placing a "kill" trigger (ID1) on the chain.

The second instance (Repeat) deals 1 damage. Imperial Decree triggers again, placing a second "kill" trigger (ID2) on the chain.

The chain resolves in LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) order:

ID2 resolves first: It attempts to kill Irelia. Guardian Angel activates as a replacement effect, destroying itself to save Irelia. Irelia is healed, exhausted, and recalled to your base.

ID1 resolves next: It attempts to kill Irelia. Because Guardian Angel has already been destroyed, there is no protection remaining. Irelia is killed at your base.

Key Nuances:

Replacement Effect: Guardian Angel is a one-time replacement effect. Once consumed to save the unit from the first kill trigger, it cannot protect against subsequent triggers.

Tracking: Imperial Decree’s kill trigger does not require the unit to remain at its original battlefield. It tracks the unit to its new location (your base) and executes the kill there.

Damage Instances: Paying the [Repeat] cost for Bellows Breath creates two distinct damage events, which is why Imperial Decree triggers twice.

question: If I first use Bellow Breath and then play Watcher, will an enemy unit of 4 might die? How does the process work?
answer:
Yes, an enemy unit with 4 Might will die in this scenario.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9019 and #10231, a unit is killed if it has marked damage equal to or greater than its current Might during a lethal damage check (which occurs after an effect resolves). Because damage remains marked on a unit and does not reduce its Might, lowering a unit's Might while it is already damaged can make that damage lethal.

Sequence of Events

Play Bellows Breath: You play Bellows Breath. As the spell resolves, you deal 1 damage to the enemy unit. This damage is "marked" on the unit.

Play Thousand-Tailed Watcher: You play the Thousand-Tailed Watcher. Its "When you play me" triggered ability is placed on the chain.

Resolve Watcher's Ability: As the ability resolves, it applies -3 Might to enemy units. The enemy unit's Might is reduced from 4 to 1.

Lethal Check: After the ability resolves, the game checks the unit's status. The unit now has 1 damage marked on it and has 1 Might. Since the marked damage (1) equals the unit's current Might (1), the unit is killed.

Key Rules

Damage vs. Might: Damage is "marked" on a unit and does not reduce its Might value. A unit dies only when marked damage meets or exceeds its current Might (CR 323.4.3b).

Resolution: Because the Watcher is played after the Bellows Breath damage is already marked, the unit's Might reduction makes the existing damage lethal.

Timing: As established in RiftJudge FAQ #3100, you cannot prevent the Thousand-Tailed Watcher's ability from resolving by killing the unit in response; the ability will still resolve even if the Watcher is removed from the board.

question: Can I play Janna, Savior in a Showdown when I am the attacker?
answer:
Yes, you can play Janna, Savior in a showdown while you are the attacker, provided you are playing her to a battlefield you control.

Reasoning

Reaction Keyword: Janna, Savior has the [Reaction] keyword, which explicitly allows her to be played at any time, including during the Closed state of a showdown.

Control Restriction: According to RiftJudge FAQ #9449, units must be played to a location you control. As the attacker in a showdown, you do not control the battlefield where the combat is taking place. However, the [Reaction] text on Janna, Savior allows her to be played "to a battlefield you control."

Therefore, as long as you are playing Janna, Savior to a battlefield you already control (a friendly battlefield), this is a legal move during the showdown. You cannot play her to the battlefield where the combat is currently taking place if that battlefield is contested and controlled by your opponent.

question: If I become the surprise defender in a showdown and that showdown ends in a combat draw, then what will happen?
answer:
According to the rules of Riftbound and the RiftJudge FAQ #4553, if a defender uses an effect to join a showdown (often called a surprise defense) and the showdown results in a draw (meaning both players have units remaining at the battlefield after combat), the attacking units are recalled to their base, and the defender remains to establish control and conquer the battlefield.

Sequence of Events:

Surprise Defense: You use a card or ability to move your unit to a battlefield already occupied by an attacker, making you the defender.

Combat Resolution: The showdown proceeds through combat.

Combat Draw: If a "draw" occurs (e.g., neither side's units are wiped out), the following steps occur during the Combat Cleanup (CR 463.1.a):

Heal all units.

Recall all attacking units (since defending units are still present at the battlefield).

Result: Because the attacking units have been recalled, you are the only player with units remaining at the battlefield.

Control: You establish control of the battlefield. If you have not yet scored this battlefield during your turn, this results in a Conquer.

This interaction holds true because the rule for recalling attacking units on a tie does not require the defender to have been in control beforehand; it only requires that a defender is present at the battlefield after combat damage has been dealt.

question: Does Teemo Strategist on defend effect happen during finalisation or resolution? I want to know whether I can react to Teemo's on defend effect after targets have been chosen.
answer:
Yes, you can react to Teemo, Strategist's "When I defend" ability after its target has been chosen.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #7962:

The triggered ability is added to the chain, and targets are chosen as the trigger is placed on the chain (during finalization).

Once the ability is on the chain with its target locked, your opponent has the opportunity to play [REACTION] cards before you begin resolving the ability (revealing cards).

Summary of Timing:

Trigger: Teemo gains the "defender" designation (e.g., when an opponent moves a unit to his battlefield).

Finalization: The "When I defend" triggered ability is added to the chain. You choose the enemy unit target at this time.

Priority Window: Because the ability is now on the chain, the state is CLOSED, and players have an opportunity to play [REACTION] cards (e.g., to move a unit, buff a unit, or remove Teemo).

Resolution: Once all players pass, the ability resolves: you reveal the top 5 cards and deal damage to the chosen target.

This is consistent with the standard FEPR process (Finalize, Execute, Pass, Resolve), where choices like targeting occur during finalization, and reactions can be played after the item is finalized but before it resolves.

question: Can I play Cull the Weak and Safety Inspector with no other minions on board?
answer:
You can play Cull the Weak even if you control no units, and you can play Safety Inspector even if you control no other units.

Playing Cull the Weak

According to multiple RiftJudge FAQs (e.g., ID 8497, 1732, 2730), you can play Cull the Weak even if you do not control any units.

Not a Target: The spell does not require you to choose a unit when it is played. The choice happens during resolution.

"Do As Much As You Can": Rule 055 states that you follow instructions as much as possible. If you control no units, you simply do not kill one, while your opponent must still fulfill their part of the effect if they control any units.

Playing Safety Inspector

Safety Inspector is a unit card. According to the <chain_rules>, units entering play enter the chain, skip Execute/Pass, and resolve immediately.

Playing with No Units: You do not need to control other units to play Safety Inspector. It is a standalone unit.

Additional Cost: The ability "You may spend 3 XP as an additional cost to play me" is optional. You may choose not to pay this cost.

"When you play me" Ability: This triggered ability uses the chain (<chain_rules>). When Safety Inspector enters play, this ability is placed on the chain.

Resolution: When the ability resolves, it instructs each player to kill one of their units. Because this is a triggered ability on a unit you just played, the "Do As Much As You Can" rule (Rule 055) applies here as well. If you control no other units (and assuming your opponent has units), you cannot kill a unit, so you ignore that part of the instruction.

If you paid the additional cost: The text "If you paid my additional cost, you don't kill a unit this way" provides you with an exemption from the effect regardless of whether you have a unit or not.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: Can you play reactions in response to a unit gaining the Attacker designation during combat?
answer:
Ruling: You cannot react to the designation itself, but you can react to the "When I attack..." triggers that result from gaining the Attacker designation. The designation is a state change that happens outside the chain, but any attack triggers it causes are placed on the chain, creating a closed state where reactions can be played.

Sequence:

A unit gains the Attacker designation during combat

Any "When I attack..." triggers are placed on the chain

The chain enters a closed state

Players may now play reaction cards in response to those triggers

Nuances:

If a unit has no "When I attack..." triggers, gaining the Attacker designation creates no reaction window since nothing enters the chain.

You are reacting to the triggered abilities on the chain, not to the designation event itself.

question: Does forbidding waste still work if a unit joins mid combat?
answer:
When a second unit joins a battlefield with Forbidding Waste, the penalty immediately stops applying.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10921, the -2 Might penalty from Forbidding Waste is a continuous static effect that is constantly re-evaluated. The battlefield checks the condition "defending alone" at all times. The moment a second friendly unit enters the battlefield, the condition is no longer met, and the -2 Might penalty is removed from your unit instantly.

Key points to remember:

Dynamic Application: Because it is a continuous effect, it does not lock in at the start of combat. It updates immediately when the game state changes.

Timing: Whether the unit enters during an Open or Closed state (during a chain), the penalty vanishes the moment the second unit is officially present at the battlefield.

Combat Damage Step: If you add a unit during combat, ensure you are tracking the unit's current Might accurately for the Combat Damage Step, as the game uses the Might values present at that time (CR 462).

question: Can a unit with ambush be played to base or does it have to be at a battlefield with a friendly unit?
answer:
You can play a unit with Ambush to your base at any time you could normally play a unit (during your Main Phase, in an Open State).

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10089:

You can always play an Ambush unit to your base, but only at normal [Action] timing.

The [Reaction] timing and the ability to play to a battlefield are conditional; they only apply when playing the unit to a battlefield where you already control units.

In summary, Ambush does not restrict you from playing the unit to your base; rather, it gives you the additional option to play it to a battlefield where you already have a presence, using [Reaction] timing.

question: Does Fiora Peerless double her might with equipment or just her own equipment?
answer:
Fiora, Peerless doubles her total Might when her ability resolves, which includes any Might bonuses she is receiving from equipment attached to her.

According to FAQ #817, Fiora's ability doubles her Might including any Might gained from passive effects like equipment (or keywords like Shield/Assault that grant Might), because those bonuses are already active when her ability triggers and resolves.

Sequence:

Combat Designation: You declare Fiora as an attacker or defender in a one-on-one combat.

Trigger: Fiora's "When I attack or defend one on one" ability triggers and is placed on the chain.

Calculation: When the trigger resolves, it looks at her current total Might (Base 3 + any active modifiers from equipment) and doubles that entire value for the duration of the combat.

This is consistent with the Arithmetic Layer system (CR 474.3), where passive increases from equipment are factored into her total Might before multiplicative effects like "Double" are applied.

question: When I proc Jhin Virtuoso Legend ability and I am at 12 runes do I get 4 floating? Or does it just ready 4?
answer:
As established by RiftJudge FAQ #9949 and RiftJudge FAQ #10084, the ability of the Jhin Legend, Virtuoso, cannot be used to exceed the maximum of 12 runes on the board.

Because you are already at the maximum of 12 runes:

The "Channel" effect fails: Channeling specifically refers to placing new runes from your deck onto the board (CR 431.1). Since you are at the maximum, the instruction to "channel 4 runes" cannot be executed and fails.

No "Ready" effect: Channeling is not equivalent to readying runes that are already on the board. The ability does not instruct you to ready any runes, so nothing will ready.

No "Floating": There is no game mechanic that converts a failed channel effect into floating energy or power.

In summary, if you are at 12 runes, the channel portion of the Virtuoso ability will simply fail to execute, and you will not gain floating resources or ready existing runes.

question: Does Relentless Pursuit allow me to move an unready unit to a battlefield?
answer:
Yes, Relentless Pursuit allows you to move an exhausted (unready) unit to a battlefield.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10072 and RiftJudge FAQ #8882, when a unit is moved by a card effect (such as Relentless Pursuit), it does not exhaust as part of the movement, and there is no requirement for the unit to be ready to be moved. Since Relentless Pursuit simply instructs you to "Move a friendly unit" without mentioning its state, an exhausted unit can be chosen and moved, and it will arrive at its destination still exhausted.

This is distinct from a "Standard Move" (Rule 144), which does require exhausting a unit as a cost. Because Relentless Pursuit moves the unit via a card effect, it bypasses that cost entirely.

question: Does heal happen on Battlefield Showdown if my damaged unit moves to an open battlefield and conquers?
answer:
No, healing does not occur in that scenario.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9649 and FAQ #9131, there is a critical distinction between a combat showdown and an open showdown:

Combat Showdown: Occurs when a unit moves to an opponent-controlled battlefield. This triggers combat, which includes a "Combat Cleanup" step where all units heal.

Open Showdown: Occurs when a unit moves to an empty (uncontrolled) battlefield. This is a showdown, but it is not combat. Because it is not combat, there is no combat cleanup, and therefore no healing occurs.

While conquering an empty battlefield allows you to score, it does not trigger the combat cleanup required to heal your units. Units only heal after combat concludes or at the end of the turn.

question: If I Wages of Pain enemy on BF and go in to attack, he flashes to go back to base, does that unit heal from combat cleanup?
answer:
Yes, the unit will still heal during the Combat Cleanup, even though it was moved back to base before combat damage could be dealt.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ (ID 8342, 4531, and 3522):

Combat is initiated the moment a unit moves to an occupied battlefield.

Once combat is initiated, all steps and phases of combat proceed, including the Combat Cleanup step.

The Combat Cleanup step triggers healing for all units in play, regardless of whether combat damage was dealt, whether the combat damage step was skipped (e.g., because a unit was moved away), or whether the unit was actually involved in the combat.

The Sequence

Initiation: You move your unit to an occupied battlefield. This initiates combat, designating the players as Attacker and Defender.

Chain/Reaction: During the resulting Showdown, your opponent plays Wages of Pain and you (or your opponent, depending on the scenario) use Flash to move a unit to base. Per RiftJudge FAQ #10310, the Flash (moving to base) resolves first, potentially making the target for Wages of Pain illegal.

Combat Cleanup: Regardless of the Wages of Pain outcome, since combat was initiated, the game proceeds to the Combat Cleanup step.

Healing: During the Combat Cleanup, all units in play (including the unit that moved back to base) heal all marked damage.

This is my interpretation based on the mechanics of Combat initiation and the provided FAQs. No official FAQ exists for this exact combination of Wages of Pain and moving during combat, but the principles of combat healing are established.

question: Does Skyfall of Areion apply to other equipment items on a unit? In this example I have Skyfall and Trinity Force attached to Lucain that just conquered so do I get two points?
answer:
Yes, you do.

According to the official Riftbound FAQs regarding the interaction between Skyfall of Areion and Trinity Force:

Equipment abilities are appended to the unit's text: When you attach equipment to a unit, that equipment's text effectively becomes part of the unit's rules text. Because of this, equipment can reference the abilities granted by other attached equipment (FAQ #225, FAQ #2017).

Skyfall of Areion's effect: This card makes the unit's "hold" effects also count as "conquer" effects, and vice versa.

Interaction result: Because Trinity Force's "When I hold, score 1 point" effect is appended to Lucian, and Skyfall makes that effect also count as a conquer effect, Lucian's conquer now triggers Trinity Force's ability.

Regarding the points:

You score 1 point from the standard game action of conquering the battlefield.

You score 1 additional point from the Trinity Force triggered ability (which is treated as a conquer effect due to Skyfall).

Total: You score 2 points total when conquering with Lucian equipped with both Trinity Force and Skyfall of Areion (FAQ #6941).

question: If I Star-Crossed a Leona Determined, does the stun still go off on my unit?
answer:
To determine if the stun still occurs, we must look at how Leona's ability interacts with the chain and the status of the game board.

The Ruling

No, the stun will not occur.

When you play Star-Crossed in response to Leona, Determined’s attack trigger, the Star-Crossed resolves first. Because Star-Crossed returns Leona to her owner's hand, she is no longer on the battlefield when her attack trigger resolves.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #2260 and #1985, when an ability referencing "here" resolves, it checks the source's location on the board. If the source (Leona) has been removed from the board (e.g., returned to hand, recalled, or defeated) before the ability resolves, its location is treated as "null." Consequently, the "here" in her ability cannot find a legal target, and the ability resolves with no effect.

The Sequence

Leona, Determined attacks: Her triggered ability ("When I attack, stun an enemy unit here") is placed on the chain.

You play Star-Crossed in response: It is placed on top of the chain.

Resolution starts:

Star-Crossed resolves: Leona and your chosen friendly unit are returned to their respective owners' hands.

Leona's attack trigger resolves: The game checks for the location "here" where Leona is. Since she is no longer on the board, the location is null.

Result: The stun effect fails to find a valid location/target and does nothing.

Note: This is my interpretation based on the mechanics of triggered abilities referencing "here" and the established FAQ rulings for Leona, Determined. No specific FAQ exists for this exact interaction with Star-Crossed, but the underlying rule regarding "null" locations applies.

question: Do you have to pay extra cost on Guards! before playing Sand Soldier to have it ready?
answer:
To determine if you must pay an extra cost on Guards! to have the Sand Soldier enter play ready, it is important to clarify that you do not have to pay the [C] (Calm power) cost to "have the Sand Soldier ready" upon playing the card. The Sand Soldier enters play as a standard unit, and the option to pay [C] is a distinct, optional instruction that occurs during the resolution of the spell.

Timing and Chain Sequence

When you play Guards! from its hidden position:

Play Phase: You play the Guards! spell, and it enters the chain.

Resolution: The spell resolves.

Step A: The first instruction is executed: "Play a 2 [S] Sand Soldier unit token." The token enters play.

Step B: The second instruction is executed: "Then do this: You may pay [C] to ready it."

Cost within instructions: As part of the resolution of the spell, you are presented with the choice to pay [C] to ready the unit. This payment is not a prerequisite to play the card or the token, but rather an optional effect to modify the state of the token upon resolution. If you choose not to pay [C], the unit remains on the board in its current state.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: Does a unit gain the Might Assault bonus on an empty battlefield?
answer:
No, a unit does not gain the might bonus from Assault when moving to an empty battlefield.

According to Rule 807.1.c, Assault is functionally short for "While I am an attacker, I have +X Might." Rule 807.1.d clarifies that a unit only gains the "Attacker" designation during Combat.

As established by RiftJudge FAQs (e.g., FAQ #9076, #863), moving a unit into an unoccupied (empty) battlefield initiates a non-combat showdown, not a combat. Because there is no opposing unit present to create combat, your unit does not receive the "Attacker" designation. Since it is not an attacker, the Assault ability remains inactive, and the might bonus is not applied.

question: When an opponent targets my Jae Medarda with a spell, do I draw a card?
answer:
Ruling: No. In Riftbound, "you" in card text refers to the controller of the card. Jae Medarda's ability "When you choose me with a spell, draw 1" only triggers when you (the controller of Jae Medarda) target her with a spell you control. When an opponent targets Jae Medarda, the ability does not trigger because the opponent is not "you" (the controller).

Nuances:

The "you" in the trigger condition refers to Jae Medarda's controller, not just any player.

If you do trigger the ability by targeting your own Jae Medarda, you draw the card as the controller of the permanent.

question: If I move Kato the Arm to a battlefield and then play an Ambush unit to that battlefield, can I give the Ambush unit the additional Might and keywords from Kato the Arm's move ability?
answer:
Ruling: No. You cannot target the Ambush unit with Kato the Arm's triggered ability because targets must be chosen when the ability is placed on the chain, before you have the opportunity to play the Ambush unit as a reaction.

Sequence:

Move Kato to a battlefield, triggering his ability

Choose targets for the ability (must choose "another friendly unit" that is already on the battlefield)

The ability becomes a chain item

Now you may play the Ambush unit as a reaction

The Ambush unit enters play, then Kato's ability resolves affecting the previously chosen target

Nuances:

If you have no other friendly units on the battlefield when Kato moves, the triggered ability is immediately removed from the chain per CR 403.3, as there are not enough valid options to make legal choices.

question: If my opponent plays Star-Crossed and I respond by playing Sacrifice targeting my own unit with Deathknell, what is the resolution order?
answer:
Ruling: The Deathknell ability resolves first, then Sacrifice, then Star-Crossed. Because killing a friendly unit is a cost for Sacrifice (paid during finalization, not resolution), the Deathknell trigger is created and added to the chain as a pending item before Sacrifice becomes finalized.

Sequence:

Opponent plays Star-Crossed (finalized on chain)

You play Sacrifice in response (added as pending item)

During Sacrifice's finalization, you pay the cost by killing your Deathknell unit

The Deathknell trigger is immediately added to the chain as a pending item

Sacrifice becomes finalized

Deathknell trigger becomes finalized (now on top of chain)

Chain resolves top-to-bottom: Deathknell → Sacrifice → Star-Crossed

Nuances:

When Star-Crossed resolves, the unit it targeted is already in the trash, so that portion of the spell fails to find a legal target and is ignored.

Costs are paid during finalization (Step 4 of playing a card), not during resolution.

question: Does "not so fast" counter both Deathknell triggers of Ruined Rex with Karthus on the field?
answer:
No, "Not So Fast" (assuming you are referring to a card effect that counters a triggered ability) will not counter both Deathknell triggers.

Why it counters only one

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9480, when you have a unit with a Deathknell ability and you control Karthus, Eternal, the Deathknell triggers twice (the base trigger plus one additional trigger from Karthus's passive ability).

These two Deathknell events are treated as separate triggers on the chain.

Separate Items: Because Karthus's ability is a passive that adds an additional instance of the trigger to the chain, each trigger is an individual item.

Targeting: If a card effect (like "Not So Fast") says "Counter target triggered ability," it targets only one specific instance on the chain. Using it once will only stop one of the two triggers; the second trigger will remain on the chain and resolve normally.

To stop both triggers, you would need to use a counter effect twice.

question: I play against Yi. I go in with Diana on a BF with one Yi. I use Moonfall to bring Akshan. Does the Yi have +2 Might from defending alone at the beginning of Showdown?
answer:
To answer your question: Yes, at the very beginning of the showdown, Master Yi's defending unit will have the +2 Might bonus, but it will lose that bonus as soon as Akshan enters the battlefield.

Here is the breakdown of why this happens based on the game rules and established FAQs:

1. Timing of the Showdown

Showdown Initiation: When your Diana, Lunari moves to the battlefield with the enemy Master Yi (or the unit being buffed by the Wuju Bladesman, Starter legend), the showdown begins.

Passive Application: The +2 Might bonus from Wuju Bladesman, Starter is a passive ability with a "While" condition ("While a friendly unit defends alone"). As confirmed in RiftJudge FAQ #10141 and FAQ #10556, this is a continuous effect that updates the game state instantaneously.

Initial State: At the moment the showdown begins, if the defending unit is currently alone on the battlefield, the game state recognizes the condition as met, and the +2 Might is applied immediately.

2. Interaction with Moonfall and Akshan

Playing Moonfall: You play Moonfall as a reaction (or action, depending on the state) to move Akshan, Mischievous to that battlefield.

Entering the Battlefield: Moonfall resolves, and Akshan moves to the battlefield.

State Update: The moment Akshan enters the battlefield, your opponent's defending unit is no longer "defending alone." The continuous "While" condition of Wuju Bladesman is no longer met.

Immediate Loss of Bonus: Per RiftJudge FAQ #10141, the game state updates instantaneously. The defending unit immediately loses the +2 Might bonus the moment Akshan arrives.

Summary of the Sequence

Showdown Begins: The battlefield is Contested. Master Yi's passive checks the board, sees the unit is alone, and grants +2 Might.

Chain: You play Moonfall. It goes on the chain.

Resolution: Moonfall resolves. Akshan enters the battlefield.

Instant Update: The board state changes (there are now two units). The Wuju Bladesman passive bonus immediately ceases to apply to the defender.

This interpretation is based on the continuous nature of passive abilities as defined in the RiftJudge FAQs #10141, #3935, and #10556.

question: Does Teemo Strategist work on all attacking units while he is defending?

question: Can I reveal a hidden Evelyn at a battlefield after my opponent plays Ruination and keep control of the battlefield?
answer:
Whether you can keep control of the battlefield depends on the state of the battlefield at the moment The Ruination resolves.

Here is the breakdown of how this interaction works:

1. Timing and Control

The Chain: When you play The Ruination, it is placed on the chain. Because there is an item on the chain, control of the battlefield cannot be lost while the chain is active (Rule 187.4.c, Unleashed update).

Revealing Evelynn: You may reveal your hidden Evelynn, Entrancing in response to The Ruination. Since Evelynn is hidden, she gains the [Reaction] keyword (Rule 811.6), allowing you to play her while the chain is closed.

Resolution: Items on the chain resolve in Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) order. If you reveal Evelynn after The Ruination has been played, Evelynn enters the battlefield, and her "When you play me from face down" triggered ability is placed on top of The Ruination on the chain.

2. Can you keep control?

Whether you keep control depends on the board state after The Ruination resolves:

The Chain Resolves:

Evelynn's trigger resolves first. If you have a target, you may move an enemy unit to her battlefield.

The Ruination resolves next, killing all units on the battlefield (including Evelynn and any unit you moved).

Post-Resolution Cleanup:

Once the chain is empty and all effects have resolved, the game checks for battlefield control.

According to CR 463.5, if there are no units remaining at that battlefield, it becomes uncontrolled.

Crucially: Even if you play Evelynn in response, The Ruination kills all units on the board. Because Evelynn will be killed by The Ruination, you will have no units remaining on the battlefield when the spell finishes resolving.

Conclusion: You cannot keep control of the battlefield. While revealing Evelynn is a legal play, The Ruination will kill Evelynn as part of its resolution, leaving the battlefield empty and thus uncontrolled.

question: Can Brynhildr be reacted to when I play it?
answer:
No, you cannot react to Brynhir Thundersong herself being played, but you can react to her "When you play me" triggered ability.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9147 and FAQ #2757:

Brynhir herself: When you play Brynhir, she resolves immediately to the battlefield. Because units resolve as soon as they are finalized to the chain, there is no window to play a reaction to the unit entering play.

Her "When you play me" effect: Once she is on the battlefield, her triggered ability goes on the chain. This is a separate event that you can respond to with reactions.

Sequence of Events

Step 1: You play Brynhir. She resolves immediately to the battlefield.

Step 2: Her "When you play me" trigger is placed on the chain.

Step 3: Players have an opportunity to play reactions in response to this trigger while it is on the chain.

Step 4: Once the trigger resolves, its effect (preventing opponents from playing cards for the remainder of the turn) takes hold. After this point, opponents can no longer play cards.

question: Can you use an action spell after somebody uses an action spell, when your unit is the only unit on the battlefield?
answer:
No, you cannot.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #8963, you cannot play an Action spell in response to an opponent's Action spell during a showdown.

Why this is the case:

Open vs. Closed State: An Action spell can only be played when the game is in an Open State (the chain is empty).

Chain Formation: When your opponent plays their Action spell, it is placed on the chain, and the game state immediately becomes Closed.

Reaction Timing: While the chain is Closed, only Reaction spells or abilities can be played. Because an Action spell requires an Open State, it cannot be played until the current chain has fully resolved and the state has returned to Open.

The Sequence:

Opponent plays an Action spell: The spell starts a chain and the state becomes Closed.

Your opportunity: Because the state is now Closed, you can only play a Reaction spell.

Resolution: Once the chain resolves and becomes empty, the state returns to Open.

Next Opportunity: After the chain is empty and the state is Open, the player with focus may then play a new Action spell.

This interpretation is based on the provided FAQ #8963 and the general mechanics of chain interactions in Riftbound.

question: I have a Kha'Zix on one battlefield, in the other one the opponent has Ferrous Runner, another unit, and a hidden. I played Void Assault to go in with Kha'Zix and move Ferrous Runner to base. So I get the +2 or no?
answer:
To determine if Kha’Zix, Mutating Horror receives the +2 Might bonus, we must look at the battlefield state at the exact moment Kha'Zix gains the "Attacker" designation.

Ruling

Yes, Kha’Zix, Mutating Horror receives the +2 Might bonus.

Reasoning

"Alone" Status: According to Rule 741.1, a unit is "alone" when there are no other friendly units at the same location. For the purpose of this condition, "friendly units" refers to those controlled by the opponent.

Hidden Cards and Unit Status: Facedown cards are considered facedown game objects rather than units. They do not gain unit properties until they are played or flipped. Therefore, a hidden card does not count as a unit present for the "alone" condition.

Timing of the Check:

Once Void Assault finishes resolving, Kha'Zix is present at the battlefield and gains the "Attacker" designation.

At the exact moment Kha'Zix gains the "Attacker" designation, the game evaluates the battlefield state. Since the hidden card is not counted as a unit, if the only remaining opponent entity is that hidden card, the "alone" condition is met.

Condition Met: Because the condition "an enemy unit is alone here" is satisfied at the moment Kha'Zix gains the Attacker designation, the ability triggers and Kha'Zix receives the +2 Might bonus.

Chain Sequence

Play Void Assault: You play Void Assault, creating a chain.

Resolution: Void Assault resolves, moving Kha'Zix to the battlefield.

Attacker Designation: Kha'Zix gains the "Attacker" designation.

Trigger Condition Check: The game checks: Is an enemy unit alone here? Because the hidden card is not a unit, the condition is satisfied.

Ability Resolution: Kha'Zix's triggered ability is placed on the chain and resolves, granting him +2 Might and 2 XP.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: Does my Star Crossed resolve or not if I play it and my opponent plays Thrill of the Hunt on that unit?
answer:
To determine whether your Star-Crossed resolves, we must look at the rules regarding targeting and zone changes.

The Ruling

Yes, your Star-Crossed will still resolve, but its effect on the unit targeted by Thrill of the Hunt will fail.

According to Rule 359.3.e.8, if a spell has more than one target and one of them becomes unavailable, the spell resolves as much as possible, operating on the remaining valid targets. However, when a unit is moved to a non-board zone (like Banishment), it ceases to be the same game object (Rule 10035). Because Thrill of the Hunt moves the unit to a non-board zone and then plays it back as a "new" game object, the targeting relationship between your Star-Crossed and that specific unit is severed.

Sequence of Events

You play Star-Crossed: You target your unit and an enemy unit. Star-Crossed is added to the chain.

Opponent plays Thrill of the Hunt: They target the enemy unit you chose. This is added to the top of the chain as a [Reaction].

Chain State (Top to Bottom):

[Top] Thrill of the Hunt

[Bottom] Star-Crossed

Resolution (LIFO - Last-In, First-Out):

Thrill of the Hunt resolves first: The unit is banished and played to a battlefield as a new game object. Because it moved to a non-board zone, the targeting relationship from Star-Crossed is severed.

Star-Crossed resolves second: It checks for its targets.

The enemy unit is no longer a legal target (it is a new object, not the one originally targeted).

Your friendly unit remains a legal target.

The spell proceeds to return your friendly unit to your hand, while the instruction to return the enemy unit is ignored as it mistargeted (Rule 359.3.e.5).

This is consistent with RiftJudge FAQ #10035, which explains that moving a unit to a non-board zone severs the targeting relationship.

question: Is there any way to react to a Glasc Mixologist getting killed by sacrifice?
answer:
Yes, you can react to a Glasc Mixologist being killed by a sacrifice effect.

According to CR 429.1.a.1.b, when a unit with a Deathknell ability is killed due to a kill instruction (such as a sacrifice effect), its Deathknell is added to the chain as a pending item before the unit is moved to the trash.

How the Interaction Works:

Kill Instruction: When the sacrifice effect (the "kill instruction") is played/activated, the Glasc Mixologist is designated as the target.

Deathknell Triggers: Before the Glasc Mixologist is actually moved to the trash, its Deathknell ability triggers and enters the chain as a pending item.

Chain State: Because an item has been placed on the chain, the game state becomes CLOSED.

Reaction Opportunity: Once the Deathknell ability is on the chain, players have the opportunity to play [Reaction] cards or activate [Reaction] abilities.

Resolution: Once all reactions are resolved, the chain resolves (LIFO). The Deathknell ability will resolve, allowing the controller of the Glasc Mixologist to play a unit from their trash.

Important Considerations:

Targeting: If you are the opponent trying to prevent the Glasc Mixologist from successfully playing a unit, you can react to the Deathknell trigger on the chain (for example, by using a card that targets the trash or interferes with the playing of the unit).

Rule Reference: Per CR 429.1.a.1.b, the game notes the information of the unit (such as its location) to process the Deathknell before the kill instruction finishes executing, ensuring the Deathknell trigger is successfully placed on the chain.

This interaction is consistent with how Deathknell abilities handle pending items on the chain, as established in the Riftbound Unleashed rules update and supported by several RiftJudge FAQs (e.g., FAQ #9783, FAQ #9149).

question: If the target of Discipline isn't in play anymore upon resolution, does the player playing it still get the draw 1? And does it work the same for Stupify and Void Seaker?
answer:
Yes, the player who played Discipline still draws 1 card, even if the targeted unit is no longer in play when Discipline resolves.

Why this happens

According to RiftJudge FAQ #10008 and Rule 359.3.e, Riftbound spells resolve as much as possible even if their target is removed or becomes illegal while the spell is on the chain.

Sequence of Events:

Play Discipline: You play Discipline, targeting your unit. It is placed on the chain.

Opponent Reacts: Your opponent plays a card that removes your unit from the battlefield (or otherwise makes it an illegal target).

Chain Resolution (LIFO - Last-In, First-Out):

The opponent's removal effect resolves first, removing your unit from the board.

Discipline then resolves. Because the instruction to "Draw 1" is not dependent on the unit successfully receiving the +2 Might, it still executes. The instruction to give the unit +2 Might is ignored because the unit is no longer a valid target (per Rule 359.3.e.5).

As noted in RiftJudge FAQ #7790, spells always resolve as much as possible, and the draw instruction does not require information about the target to successfully resolve.

question: Can my opponent use Sacrifice on Glasc Mixologist and can I react with Star Cross to cancel Sacrifice?
answer:
No, you cannot use Star-Crossed to cancel your opponent's Sacrifice.

The Ruling

In Riftbound, "canceling" a spell or ability is not a standard mechanic. The only way to stop a spell or ability from resolving is to Counter it, and Star-Crossed does not have an effect that counters spells.

Countering: Per CR 426.2.a, you can only Counter a card or ability when specifically directed to do so by a card effect (e.g., a card that says "Counter target spell").

Star-Crossed: Its text states: "Return a friendly unit and an enemy unit to their owners' hands." It does not contain a "Counter" instruction. Even if you target the Glasc Mixologist with Star-Crossed, the Sacrifice spell has already been finalized on the chain, and its costs (including killing the Glasc Mixologist) have already been paid (Rule 357.4). Returning the Glasc Mixologist to hand after it has already been killed as a cost does not remove Sacrifice from the chain.

Sequence of Events

If your opponent plays Sacrifice and you respond with Star-Crossed:

Opponent plays Sacrifice: They pay the additional cost by killing their Glasc Mixologist. Sacrifice is finalized and added to the chain.

You play Star-Crossed: You add Star-Crossed to the top of the chain as a [Reaction].

Resolution (LIFO - Last-In, First-Out):

Star-Crossed resolves: It attempts to return the targeted units to hands. If Glasc Mixologist is already in the trash (because it was killed as the cost for Sacrifice), that part of the instruction will fail to find a valid target and be ignored (Rule 359.3.e.5).

Sacrifice resolves: Even though the Glasc Mixologist is no longer on the board, Sacrifice has already been successfully played and its costs paid. Your opponent will proceed to draw 2 cards and channel 1 rune.

This is my interpretation based on the mechanics of costs and resolution in Riftbound. No official FAQ exists for this exact scenario, but it aligns with the handling of costs and invalid targets defined in Rules 357.4 and 359.3.e.

question: Can I play Grim Apothecary, trigger effect on itself, react with Rengar Legend effect on another unit and take back to hand the Apothecary?
answer:
Yes, you can do this.

As the controller of both the Grim Apothecary "When you play me" trigger and the Pridestalker (Rengar Legend) trigger (both triggered by the same event: playing a unit), you choose the order in which they are placed on the chain. To achieve your goal, you should order them so that the Grim Apothecary trigger is at the bottom and the Pridestalker trigger is on top.

Sequence:

Play Grim Apothecary: You play the unit; it enters the battlefield.

Triggers: Both the Grim Apothecary "When you play me" ability and the Pridestalker ability trigger.

Place on Chain: You, as the controller, place them on the chain. You place the Grim Apothecary ability on the chain first, then place the Pridestalker ability on top.

Chain State: The state is now Closed.

Resolution (LIFO):

Pridestalker ability resolves: You choose a unit (e.g., another unit on your battlefield) and give it +1 Might.

Grim Apothecary ability resolves: You make your choice for the "you may" effect. Since Grim Apothecary is a friendly unit on the battlefield, it is a legal target. You may choose to return Grim Apothecary to your hand.

Key Rules Supporting this:

Simultaneous Triggers (Rule 383.3.d): When multiple triggered abilities you control trigger simultaneously, you decide the order they are placed on the chain.

LIFO Resolution: The chain resolves from top to bottom (Last-In, First-Out).

Grim Apothecary Target (FAQ 9746): Grim Apothecary can target itself, as it is a "friendly unit" once it is in play.

Pridestalker (FAQ 9769): You can target any unit with Pridestalker's ability.

Note: This interpretation assumes you have the required energy to play Grim Apothecary and that you are in a situation where you can play it (such as having sufficient energy and being in your Main Phase if playing it normally, or meeting Ambush conditions).

question: I just guessed a target opponent plays a reaction to get it over 3 might, I have a Ravenbloom Student, does she get +1?
answer:
Yes, your Ravenbloom Student will get +1 Might in this scenario.

According to Rule 359.3.e.10, if all targets for a spell become invalid (such as the target's Might increasing above the allowed limit while the spell is on the stack), the spell has no effect but is still considered "played." Because the spell is still considered "played," "When you play a spell" triggered abilities, such as the Ravenbloom Student’s, will still trigger.

In your situation, you have played Gust. Here is the sequence of events:

Finalization: You play Gust, targeting an enemy unit. You pay the energy cost.

Reaction: Your opponent plays a reaction to increase the target's Might above 3.

Resolution of Reaction: The reaction resolves first. The target is now at 4 Might (or higher).

Resolution of Gust: Gust resolves. Because the target is now above 3 Might, the targeting restriction of Gust is no longer met. As per Rule 359.3.e.10, the spell has no effect, but it is still considered "played."

Trigger Condition: Because the spell is considered "played," the Ravenbloom Student’s triggered ability triggers and grants it +1 Might.

Note: I could not fully verify this ruling against the retrieved rules.

question: When I play Akshan and steal a tapped gear, does it stay tapped or untapped?
answer:
When you use Akshan's ability to steal a piece of gear, the gear's status (tapped/exhausted or untapped/ready) does not change.

According to the core mechanics of Riftbound, when you gain control of a permanent, it retains its current state (exhausted or ready) unless a card effect specifically instructs you to change it. Because Akshan's ability only moves the gear to your base and changes its controller, the gear remains in the same tapped (exhausted) state it was in before it was stolen.

Note: This is my interpretation based on standard game mechanics regarding control-change and state. No official FAQ exists for this specific interaction regarding the state of stolen gear.

question: Smoke Screen on a Rift Herald then Gust on the same reaction chain, does the Gust resolve before the Smoke Screen and make the Rift Herald not mighty? If not, can you react with sacrifice to kill the Rift Herald before Gust resolves?
answer:
To determine the resolution of this chain, we must follow the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) rule for chain resolution.

The Chain Sequence

Smoke Screen is played targeting your Rift Herald. It is added to the chain.

Gust is played as a reaction, also targeting Rift Herald. It is added to the top of the chain.

The chain currently looks like this (from bottom to top):

Smoke Screen

Gust (Top)

Resolution

Does Gust resolve before Smoke Screen? Yes. Because Gust was added to the chain after Smoke Screen, it is the topmost item and resolves first.

Will Rift Herald be returned to your hand? Yes, provided Rift Herald has 3 or less Might when Gust resolves.

Will Smoke Screen's effect apply? No. After Gust resolves, the Rift Herald will have been returned to your hand. When Smoke Screen attempts to resolve, it will fail to find its target (it has changed zones to a non-board zone). The instruction will be ignored (Rule 359.3.e.5).

Can you sacrifice Rift Herald?

If you have an ability that requires sacrificing a unit as a cost (e.g., a "Kill a friendly unit" effect), you can indeed activate it while the chain is in a closed state.

Sequence:

Chain: Smoke Screen (bottom), Gust (top).

You activate a sacrifice-based ability in response to Gust. The chain is now: Smoke Screen, Gust, [Your Ability].

[Your Ability] resolves first: You sacrifice Rift Herald to pay the cost.

Gust resolves next: Because its target (Rift Herald) has left the battlefield and is no longer a legal target, Gust "whiffs" (does nothing).

Smoke Screen resolves last: It also fails to find its target (the unit is in the trash) and does nothing.

Summary:

Gust resolves first. It will bounce the Rift Herald to your hand if it has 3 or less Might.

You can sacrifice the Rift Herald in response to Gust. If you do, both Gust and Smoke Screen will fail to resolve because their target is no longer on the battlefield.

This is my interpretation based on the mechanics of the LIFO chain and targeting rules. No official FAQ exists for this specific interaction.

question: Can I chain Zhonyas to my Lonely Poro Deathnell out of Showdown if they use Singularity on Lonely Poro?
answer:
Yes, you can react to the Lonely Poro Deathknell trigger with Zhonya's Hourglass, but there is a crucial timing distinction to understand regarding how Zhonya's works.

Can you react?

Yes. When your Lonely Poro dies and its Deathknell trigger is placed on the chain, the game state becomes "Closed." This opens a window where you can play [Reaction] cards. Since Zhonya's Hourglass can be played from hidden (which functions as a [Reaction]), you can certainly play it in response to the Deathknell trigger.

Will it save the Lonely Poro?

No. Zhonya's Hourglass is a replacement effect. For it to save a unit, it must be active at the moment the death event occurs to replace that death with "kill this instead."

By the time the Lonely Poro Deathknell trigger is on the chain, the unit is already dead and has been sent to the trash (or is in the process of being sent there). The Deathknell trigger is simply the result of that death having already happened. Because the death has already occurred, the replacement window has closed, and Zhonya's Hourglass cannot retroactively prevent that death.

How it resolves (LIFO)

Event: Singularity deals 6 damage to Lonely Poro. Lonely Poro dies, and its Deathknell trigger is added to the chain.

Reaction: You play your hidden Zhonya's Hourglass. It is added to the top of the chain.

Resolution:

Zhonya's Hourglass resolves: It enters the battlefield (or is played as gear), but since there is no longer a death event to replace, it simply enters play.

Lonely Poro Deathknell resolves: You draw 1 card (assuming it died alone, as per the Deathknell condition).

Summary: You can play the Zhonya's to get it onto the board, but it will not save the Lonely Poro because the death has already finalized by the time the Deathknell trigger is on the chain. You will still get your Deathknell draw, provided the condition of being "alone" was met at the time of death.

question: Do I need another friendly unit to play Beast Below?
answer:
No, you do not need another friendly unit to play Beast Below.

According to the RiftJudge FAQ (#466, #9370, #9889):

Playing the Unit: You are permitted to play Beast Below as a unit even if you do not control another friendly unit.

Triggered Ability: Its "When you play me" ability requires you to target another friendly unit and an enemy unit. Because valid targets must exist for all required targets to place an object on the chain, if you do not control another friendly unit, you simply do not put the triggered ability on the chain.

Result: The unit enters the battlefield normally, and the ability—which would have returned units to their owners' hands—never triggers or enters the chain, so your unit remains on the battlefield.

question: When Vex Apathetic is at the battlefield and Elder Drake is played, does he still do damage?
answer:
Yes, Elder Dragon still deals damage and its passive ability will still function, even if it is stunned by Vex, Apathetic.

Here is the breakdown of the interaction:

The Sequence of Events

Playing Elder Dragon: The opponent plays the Elder Dragon. Its "When you play me" triggered ability is placed on the chain.

Vex's Trigger: Vex, Apathetic's ability ("When an opponent plays a unit...") triggers and is placed on the chain.

Chain Resolution: The chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) order.

Vex’s ability resolves first, programmatically selecting the Elder Dragon and applying the Stun effect.

Elder Dragon’s "When you play me" ability then resolves, dealing 1 damage to the chosen enemy units.

Why Elder Dragon still functions:

Stun vs. Passive Abilities: According to RiftJudge FAQ #10447, a stunned unit cannot contribute its Might to combat damage (CR 424.1.b), but being stunned does not deactivate a unit's passive abilities. Because Elder Dragon's ability ("Any amount of your damage is enough to kill enemy units") is a passive ability, it remains active even while the unit is stunned.

Dealing Damage: The damage dealt by Elder Dragon’s "When you play me" ability is a separate game action from combat damage. Since the ability triggers and resolves as part of playing the card (which happens before Vex's stun would have any impact on the Elder Dragon's ability to "attack"), the Elder Dragon successfully deals its damage.

Summary: Vex, Apathetic will successfully stun the Elder Dragon, preventing it from moving or contributing its Might to combat damage during the Combat Damage Step, but it does not stop the Elder Dragon from dealing the damage specified by its "When you play me" ability, nor does it deactivate the Elder Dragon's passive ability.

question: Does The List work for Ezreal's legend ability when exhausting it?
answer:
No, The List does not count toward Ezreal’s legend ability.

The Ruling

Ezreal’s legend ability requires that you have chosen enemy units and/or gear twice this turn with spells or unit abilities.

In Riftbound, there is a formal distinction between ability categories:

Unit Abilities: Triggered or activated abilities originating from a unit (Rule 145).

Gear Abilities: Triggered or activated abilities originating from gear (Rule 150).

Because Ezreal’s legend ability specifically limits the qualifying sources to "spells or unit abilities," an activated ability originating from a piece of gear does not contribute to the "chosen twice" requirement.

Why it does not work

Categorization: Per Rule 145 and Rule 150, the game treats unit abilities and gear abilities as distinct categories.

Specific Phrasing: Ezreal’s legend ability uses restrictive phrasing. In Riftbound, when a card specifies the source of an interaction (e.g., "unit abilities"), that restriction is authoritative.

No FAQ Override: There is no official Riftbound ruling or FAQ entry that classifies gear abilities as unit abilities.

Summary: Since The List functions as a gear card, its ability is classified as a gear ability. It does not meet the "unit ability" requirement specified in Ezreal’s legend ability text.

Note: I could not fully verify the classification of 'The List' against the retrieved rules.

question: If my opponent plays Elder Dragon and targets my unit on the bf with its effect but I flash my unit back to base, does my unit still die?
answer:
Your unit will live.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #9919 and the Rules FAQ Clarification (2026-04-29), Elder Dragon's "When you play me" ability has specific targeting restrictions based on location. It targets "up to one enemy unit at [a specific location]."

The Sequence of Events:

Playing the Ability: When your opponent plays Elder Dragon, its "When you play me" ability is placed on the chain. Your opponent must lock in targets at specific locations (e.g., "the unit at Battlefield 1").

Reacting: You play Flash in response. Because Flash is a [REACTION], it is added to the chain on top of Elder Dragon's ability.

Resolution Order: The chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) order. Flash resolves first, moving your unit to your base.

Check on Resolution: When Elder Dragon's ability attempts to resolve, it checks the location of its target. Because your unit moved to your base, it no longer fulfills the targeting restriction of the ability (which required the unit to be at the battlefield).

Result: Your unit is no longer a valid target for that specific location-based instruction and is unaffected by the damage.

As stated in the official clarification: "If you play Flash in reaction to the play effect of Elder Dragon, any units that are moved to a location other than the one where they were targeted will no longer fulfill the targeting restriction of the Elder Dragon play effect and will be unaffected by the ability as it resolves."

Note: This ruling is based on the mechanics of location-based targeting as clarified in the Riftbound rules updates.

question: If I'm attacking a battlefield with Ezreal, and my opponent has a Yuumi, who's attacking/defending trigger resolves first?
answer:
In a combat showdown, the order in which triggered abilities resolve is determined by the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle as applied to the chain. Because the defender adds their triggers to the chain after the attacker, the defender’s trigger will resolve first, and the attacker’s trigger will resolve last.

The Trigger Sequence

According to Rule 383.4 and CR 443.1.b.1:

Placement on the Chain:

The Attacking player places their triggered abilities on the chain first.

The Defending player places their triggered abilities on the chain last.

Resolution Order (LIFO):

Because the defender’s triggered abilities are added to the chain after the attacker’s, the defending player's triggered ability resolves first.

The attacking player's triggered ability resolves second.

question: Does removing a unit in reaction chain prevent its when I'm played ability from activating?
answer:
No, removing a unit in response to its "When I'm played" ability does not prevent that ability from activating or resolving.

According to RiftJudge FAQ #8020 and FAQ #5217:

"When you play me" abilities (Play Effects) still resolve even if the unit is killed, bounced, or banished by a reaction to that ability.

Once a unit with a Play Effect is played, the unit enters the board immediately. The Play Effect then triggers, enters the chain, and provides a window for players to play reactions.

Triggered abilities resolve independently of their source. While effects within the ability that reference the unit itself (e.g., "this unit," "here," or location-based references) may fail if the unit is no longer in play or at the correct location, the rest of the ability's instructions will still execute to the fullest extent possible.

The Sequence

Following RiftJudge FAQ #6781 and Core Rule 383.4.a.2, the sequence is as follows:

Play: You play the unit card. It enters the chain and is immediately finalized to the board.

Trigger: Because the unit has a "When I'm played" ability, that ability triggers and is placed on the chain as a pending item.

Reaction Window: The state is now CLOSED (a chain exists). Players can now play [REACTION] cards to respond to the triggered ability.

Removal: If you use a reaction to remove the unit, the triggered ability remains on the chain.

Resolution: When players pass, the chain resolves (LIFO). The triggered ability resolves, performing as many of its instructions as possible.

question: If Irresistible Faefolk moves to an empty battlefield and chooses to move an enemy unit in, and the enemy wants to cast Gust, is the Gust castable before or after the enemy unit is moved in?
answer:
When you move Irresistible Faefolk to an unoccupied battlefield, the sequence proceeds as follows:

Trigger: The "When I move to a battlefield..." triggered ability of Irresistible Faefolk is placed on the chain.

Priority Window: A priority window opens while this ability is on the chain. Your opponent may cast Gust at this time as a reaction, provided the target meets its requirements (a unit at a battlefield with 3 Might or less).

Resolution: The chain resolves in Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) order. If your opponent cast Gust, it resolves first, potentially removing your Irresistible Faefolk or another valid target from the battlefield.

Trigger Resolution: The Faefolk's ability resolves. You choose an enemy unit and move it to that battlefield.

Combat Transition: If an enemy unit is moved into the battlefield, it becomes contested and a Combat Showdown begins. Players receive a priority window to cast spells (such as Gust) after the Faefolk's ability resolves but before the showdown proceeds to deal combat damage.

Summary

Your opponent can cast Gust in response to the triggered ability while it is on the chain, or they may cast it after the enemy unit has been moved in but before the showdown resolves.

question: Can you use a unit with ganking at a battlefield after a showdown?
answer:
Yes, a unit with Ganking can move to another battlefield after participating in a showdown, provided the unit is ready (unexhausted).

According to RiftJudge FAQ #1961:

"Ruling: If a unit with Ganking is ready (unexhausted) after a showdown, you can use the Standard Move Action to move it to another battlefield during your turn. There does not need to be an enemy unit at the destination battlefield."

Important context for this interaction:

Showdowns do not exhaust units: Participating in a showdown does not automatically exhaust your units, meaning they remain ready to perform a Standard Move after the showdown concludes, provided they weren't exhausted for another cost earlier in the turn.

Timing: You must perform this move during your Main Phase, while the game is in an Open State (there is no chain currently resolving, and no active showdown or combat ongoing at that specific location).

Standard Move restriction: You cannot move units using Ganking (or any Standard Move) while a showdown is currently in progress (Rule 143.1.c). You must wait until the showdown has concluded.

question: Do I have to use Leblanc Deceiver's ability when I conquer or hold, or anytime as long as the condition was met?
answer:
You do not have to use LeBlanc's "Deceiver" ability.

According to the card text, the ability is optional: "...you may discard 1 and exhaust me..."

Because the ability includes the phrase "you may," it is an optional triggered ability. When you conquer or hold a battlefield, you decide whether or not to place the ability on the chain. If you choose not to place it on the chain at that time, it simply does not trigger for that instance of conquering or holding.

As clarified in RiftJudge FAQ #10377: "Because the ability text uses 'you may,' the trigger is optional. When you conquer or hold, you decide whether or not to place the ability on the chain."

question: Who draws the card?

question: If Pyke dies and an enemy unit dies at the same time, does Pyke still grant 1 gold?
